#1209. Enzo Maresca's ref rage: Man City boss claims recent decisions are worst he has 'ever seen' as he becomes latest manager to hit out at officials

Published: 11:59 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 14:35 EST, 27 November 2026

Enzo Maresca has echoed Mauricio Pochettino’s punchy criticism of refereeing displays by claiming that some recent decisions against Manchester City are among the worst he has ever witnessed.

The absorbing rivalry between titans Erling Haaland and Gabriel – a battle renowned for excessive physicality - returns when City go to Premier League champions Arsenal on Sunday.

And Maresca suggested that key calls in City’s recent winless run have contributed to them falling six points behind Mikel Arteta’s leaders.

Asked whether Haaland is treated unfairly by officials, the Italian said: ‘I can see that, to be honest. I can see also more things in the last four or five games - probably since the international break.

‘I’ve never seen in my life a player touch the ball with both arms and no penalty. For instance against Brighton, (Lewis) Dunk. I never seen it in my life. If you remember, both. No penalty. The other one was like volleyball.’

The second complaint from that Brighton defeat was an appeal for handball against Lukas Vuskovic, when Diego Gomez headed into the defender’s outstretched arm. The league’s Key Match Incidents panel voted 3-2 in favour of Craig Pawson’s decision not to award a penalty for Dunk’s handball.

Maresca suggested that key calls in City’s recent winless run have contributed to them falling six points behind Mikel Arteta’s leaders

New Manchester United boss Pochettino said last weekend that with VAR, the league possesses ‘the best car but we need to drive it in the right way’ following Leny Yoro’s sending off at Liverpool.

Maresca’s analysis also partly centred on how VAR is being used as he raised Haaland’s disallowed goal against Fulham at the weekend, when the striker was adjudged to have fouled Bernd Leno and VAR stuck with the on-field decision.

‘The last game against Fulham, if you just stop (the image) when the goalkeeper has the ball there, it looks like (a foul), but the dynamic is he is not catching the ball,’ Maresca added.

‘Even the keeper does not believe that he was. Yes, there are fouls for Erling, but I can see also in the last games from the international break things that I don’t like, that for me are clear. But the referee is there, they decide, so we need to adapt.’

Haaland has talked up his enthusiasm for going up against Gabriel this week and should be reinvigorated for the challenge after cutting a forlorn figure during and after the 2-2 draw with Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday.

The 26-year-old appeared downbeat during media interviews immediately after the game, sparking a discussion over his current frame of mind.

Maresca insisted that the striker’s mood is in line with other players as they strive to break free of a disappointing set of performances.

‘Erling is a winner,’ the City manager said. ‘It's normal that he's not happy when we don't win games but it’s not just Erling, it's everyone. Don't forget that two weeks ago or three weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch (after beating Brighton in the Carabao Cup).

Asked whether Haaland is treated unfairly by officials, the Italian said: ‘I can see that, to be honest. I can see also more things in the last four or five games'

‘You can write or think many different things, but the reality is sometimes much easier: Erling is upset, like I'm upset because we're not winning games. And when we were winning games everyone was happy. But this is our job, this is football, that's why we need to maintain the balance.’

Haaland has admitted that he needs to improve in front of goal after scoring just once in his last five club games, yet Maresca believes the problems instead lie in quality consistent service.

‘I think he is gesticulating in the same way when we were winning games and he was not receiving balls,’ he said. ‘Erling is a No 9, the No 9’s live day by day for goals.

‘When we drop the opposition inside the box and he is inside the box, he is the king there. The problem is that most of the teams now, because they are so aggressive, they come higher on the pitch, so you need him also to link a little bit. We need him in different ways.

‘I'm not a magician, there is a transition here. It's normal. We have eight, nine new players, manager is new - you need time. You see at different clubs when they had transitions, how complicated it is.’

Manchester United are reportedly keeping a close eye on Nico Paz, although Fabrizio Romano has downplayed speculation linking the Como star to a move to Old Trafford amid growing interest in the Argentine playmaker.

The 22-year-old has established himself as one of the most exciting young midfielders in European football, drawing attention from several top clubs after impressive performances in Italy.

Romano has clarified United’s interest in Paz, suggesting the links are largely driven by the connection between the player’s representatives and new head coach Mauricio Pochettino.

The transfer expert explained that the agency representing Pochettino also manages Paz, fueling speculation about a possible move to the Premier League.

United are understood to admire the Como star, but there is currently no concrete progress towards a transfer, with neither negotiations nor direct contact taking place between the parties.

“Get ready [for] the links between Nico Paz and Manchester United for one reason: Nico Paz is represented by the same agency of Mauricio Pochettino,” Romano said on YouTube.

“For sure, Manchester United appreciate Nico Paz. But, all the top clubs in Europe are following and appreciating Nico Paz.

“It’s Man Utd, more English clubs – don’t forget that Tottenham tried in summer 2025 – there are clubs also from other countries.

“He’s absolutely shining for Como and for the Argentina national team. This boy is special. So, it’s obvious that all these top clubs are looking at Nico Paz.

“Manchester United are following Nico Paz closely. They were falling in love with Nico Paz when he played against them in Como.

“The links with Man Utd are stronger for one reason: the agency representing Pochettino and Nico Paz. But that doesn’t mean it’s going to be Nico Paz to Man Utd just because he has the same agent.

“Let me clarify also [that] in the January window, according to my information, there will be zero movement with Nico Paz.

“So, when we talk about Nico Paz, we talk about the summer. Nico Paz in January is 100 per cent staying at Como.”

Paz has been in outstanding form for Como, and his technical ability, creativity and attacking intelligence have made him an attractive prospect for several European giants.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Romano has also stressed that Real Madrid remain in control of the midfielder’s situation, with the Spanish giants possessing an €80 million buy-back clause that becomes active in summer 2027.

Los Blancos are reportedly keen to bring the Argentine back to the Bernabeu, although Paz previously opted to stay at Como rather than return to Madrid immediately.

The midfielder is expected to stay in Italy for the remainder of the campaign, ruling out a January transfer to Manchester United or any other club.

United could revisit their interest next summer, but they will face competition from several European sides for his signature.

Paz’s future will ultimately depend on Real Madrid’s plans and the player’s own decision when the season concludes.

#1207. Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Quantum metrology promises measurement precision beyond classical limits by exploiting large-scale quantum states1,2,3,4,5,6,7, yet realizing this advantage faces two fundamental challenges: the deterministic preparation of non-trivial quantum probes8,9 and the efficient extraction of metrological information in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces10,11,12. Here, we introduce quantum confocal microscopy in Fock space that addresses these challenges for a Fock-like probe state with a tightly concentrated photon-number distribution. Drawing a direct analogy between classical wave optics and quantum state evolution in a bosonic mode13,14, we construct a confocal lens system with a quantum circuit of \({\mathcal{O}}(1)\) operational depth, realizing a bidirectional transformation between a readily obtainable coherent state and this Fock-like probe state. Using a superconducting circuit quantum electrodynamics platform, we deterministically prepare focused probe states with mean photon numbers up to N = 500, achieving a 21.5 ± 1.1 dB reduction of the photon-number variance relative to a coherent state. Using the focused states for displacement sensing, we achieve a record metrological gain of 19.20 ± 0.20 dB beyond the standard quantum limit. This work establishes quantum confocal microscopy as a compact protocol that makes high-photon-number non-Gaussian Fock-like probes experimentally accessible and measurable, providing a viable route towards quantum-enhanced precision measurement, and is readily extendable to other bosonic platforms and high-dimensional quantum many-body systems.

#1206. Spotlight on Jones as Inter await impact from ex-Liverpool midfielder

Il Corriere dello Sport notes that Curtis Jones has yet to justify his €30m price tag at Inter this season, yet the Nerazzurri hope the ex-Liverpool midfielder will follow the same trajectory as his compatriot Djed Spence.

Jones has recently returned to action after recovering from an adductor injury that sidelined him for a month.

The English midfielder hasn’t scored or assisted in seven appearances across all competitions for Inter this season and has started only twice.

His slow start to the 2026-27 campaign was one of the topics on today’s front page of Corriere dello Sport.

The Italian sports newspaper (via FCInternews) notes that the 25-year-old hasn’t yet made his mark with the Nerazzurri this season, but coach Cristian Chivu still has faith in the ex-Liverpool midfielder and is expected to give him another chance in tonight’s Serie A match against Genoa.

The Nerazzurri will play the Grifone twice in four days as the two teams will also meet in the Coppa Italia Round of 16 next Tuesday and Jones will likely start both matches.

Inter and Chivu hope Jones will follow the same trajectory as his compatriot Spence, who missed the season’s opening games to recover match fitness.

The ex-Tottenham man, however, has now become a starter for the Nerazzurri, although he might rest against his former club Genoa tonight, providing two assists in his first nine matches with the defending Serie A champions.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola has revealed that midfielder Ryan Gravenberch is unlikely to be available for Sunday’s Premier League Merseyside derby clash against Everton at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The 24-year-old Netherlands international has been sidelined since Liverpool’s 1-0 home defeat to Arsenal on November 1 and had been hoping to return in time for the clash against their local rivals.

However, speaking during his pre-match press conference at the AXA Training Centre, Iraola admitted that the fixture will almost certainly come too soon for Gravenberch, who joins Cody Gakpo on the sideline.

“It’s going to be difficult. I cannot say no [his availability for Sunday’s match]. But it’s difficult, he is dealing with this situation. Important thing is he is back with no pain to play as free as possible.”

Gravenberch’s injury frustration comes amid with growing uncertainty surrounding his long-term Anfield future.

The Dutch international only signed a six-year contract extension in March 2026, committing his future to Liverpool until 2032.

However, recent reports have suggested that his agent, José Fortes Rodriguez, has made informal contact with several leading European clubs to gauge potential transfer interest.

Given the length of his contract, the Reds remain in a particularly strong negotiating position should any interested club come forward.

Nevertheless, the speculation adds another layer of uncertainty to what has been a frustrating, injury-disrupted campaign for the Dutchman so far.

While Gravenberch has been recovering from injury, Liverpool’s exciting teenage midfielder Trey Nyoni has continued to make significant strides under Iraola.

The 19-year-old became Liverpool’s second-youngest Champions League goalscorer when he found the net against Fenerbahçe earlier this month.

He followed that up with another composed performance in Wednesday’s 3-0 Champions League victory over Club Brugge, playing 73 minutes as Liverpool secured an impressive win in Belgium.

Nyoni’s composure in possession, technical ability and willingness to take responsibility at such a young age have been particularly encouraging.

Liverpool are also reportedly preparing improved contract terms for the England Under-21 international, reflecting his growing importance to the club’s long-term plans.

While Gravenberch remains an established first-team player, Nyoni’s emergence has given Iraola another exciting option in midfield.

#1204. David Raya MISSES training ahead of Arsenal's crunch clash with Man City in blow for Mikel Arteta

Published: 14:47 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 14:53 EST, 27 November 2026

David Raya didn’t take part in Arsenal’s training session today, plunging into doubt his availability for Sunday’s Premier League showdown against Manchester City.

Raya appeared to be in agony as he was forced off in the 70th minute of Arsenal’s 2-2 draw at Newcastle last Saturday, hurting his left shoulder in an accidental collision with William Osula.

There were initial fears the goalkeeper could be facing an extended spell on the sidelines, with Kepa Arrizabalaga playing in Tuesday’s Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund.

Raya appeared in agony after hurting his left shoulder in a collision with William Osula

Yet Mikel Arteta this afternoon alluded to there being a chance Raya would be fit enough to play on Sunday, replying ‘yeah’ when asked if he was hopeful of the goalkeeper’s availability.

He also said: ‘Yeah, they're all training. Bukayo (Saka) as well is training…’, alluding to the individual work the winger is doing away from the main group.

When asked, ‘is he (Raya) diving around?’ Arteta replied: ‘(On) that, I'm not sure.’

His absence from the training session doesn’t rule the goalkeeper out of Sunday’s fixture, but significant doubts remain over whether Raya will be fit to face Man City.

#1203. Ex-Juventus players deliver Ekhator verdict after first Juventus goal

Jeff Ekhator scored his first Juventus goal on Thursday, and five ex-Bianconeri players share their verdicts on the 20-year-old who was deployed as a centre-forward earlier this week.

The Italian starlet scored on his debut as a starter on Thursday, helping the Old Lady win 4-1 against Omonoia FC in the Europa League.

The versatile Italian talent mostly played as a winger and support striker at Genoa before joining Juventus last summer.

However, with Juventus coach Luciano Spalletti looking for a classic centre-forward, Ekhator was used as a No. 9, and the 20-year-old responded positively.

Ekhator had a tough start to the season, missing three months of action due to muscular problems. He has made only three Juventus appearances so far, but the signals he sent in his first start earlier this week were surely encouraging.

This, at least, is what five ex-Juventus players feel. La Gazzetta dello Sport, in fact, questioned Massimo Mauro, Vincenzo Iaquinta, Vincenzo Padovano, Nicola Amoruso and Emanuele Giaccherini on the 20-year-old attacker’s performance, and all of them had positive impressions.

At the same time, however, they stressed that Ekhator should not be given all the pressure for Juventus’ results and performances, especially at a moment when the Bianconeri are rebuilding.

Ekhator joined Juventus from Genoa last summer in a €16m deal plus add-ons and signed a contract until June 2031.

Here’s what the ex-Juventus players had to say.

Mauro: “I think Jeff is an excellent player. In a Juve side performing at its best, he would obviously learn much faster. Let’s see how regularly he gets to play. Against Omonoia FC, he received a wonderful pass and scored. He did well, but that shows the whole team needs to raise its level: neither he nor anyone else in the squad will solve Juventus’ problems single-handedly.”

Iaquinta: “I think it’s too early to know whether Ekhator can really be Juventus’ No.9 for the future. Surely, he already has a role to play now, which is significant for someone who has only just turned 20. What I’ve seen—particularly the other night in the Europa League—is encouraging, because Ekhator still has room to improve. What I like about him is his desire to keep making runs in behind, which requires real physical strength and power in your legs. I think he’ll carve out a role for himself, partly because I can see him playing alongside either Woltemade or Kolo Muani.”

Padovano: “I’ve followed Ekhator since his time in Genoa’s youth academy: he knows how to attack space, protects the ball well and is physically strong. I think he could be very useful to Juventus, given their shortcomings up front and the lack of a centre-forward in the squad. He’s 20 and needs time to develop, but he has tremendous quality. That said, some players are already stars at that age. He has a huge opportunity: he took his first chance, and now he needs to build on it consistently. Ekhator has the qualities of the No.9 they’re missing, and Spalletti will give him more and more playing time. His goal against Omonoia FC was a true striker’s finish. What Juventus are looking for is already in their ranks.”

Amoruso: “We’re talking about a very young player, although he has qualities that impress me: he makes good runs in behind, has plenty of power in his legs and makes the right movements. He also played as a second striker at Genoa, but I think Ekhator has everything it takes to become a great centre-forward. Given that Spalletti often plays Kolo Muani and Woltemade together, I would have little doubt that he could also play alongside either of them. What matters, though, is that nobody expects a 20-year-old to be the answer to all Juventus’ problems, because that would place an enormous burden on his shoulders. Ekhator needs to be allowed to develop without pressure, because he has the quality to become a leading figure at Juve in the future.”

Giaccherini: “Jeff is young but, in some respects, ‘experienced’: he arrived at Juventus with more than 50 Serie A appearances, no small tally for a 20-year-old. At a Juventus side forever searching for a ‘true’ No.9, Ekhator can aim to carve out a role for himself and potentially become a regular starter in that position. His movement helps the team, his physical strength allows him to receive the ball onto his feet under pressure, and then he does what a ‘true’ number nine does: one shot, his first, and a goal. Let’s not forget that he played alongside Pio Esposito in Crete when Baldini was interim national-team coach. He’s a modern striker—let’s put our faith in him.”

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

Roberto De Zerbi has outlined Tottenham’s future transfer plans, revealing that he believes the club are just three or four positions away from completing his squad rebuild.

Tottenham were among the biggest spenders during the summer transfer window, with the club’s hierarchy heavily backing the Italian following their disappointing campaign last season.

And despite a difficult start to the new season, Spurs are beginning to show encouraging signs of progress under De Zerbi, having won four of their last five Premier League matches.

Speaking ahead of Sunday’s trip to Sunderland, the 47-year-old expressed his satisfaction with the business Tottenham conducted in the summer while revealing what the club still need to do in the transfer market.

He said (quotes via Football London): “As a team, as a squad, I think we are in a very good position because we made a great session of the transfer market. We changed 10 players, and we brought all first targets in the window.

“For the future, we don’t need in too many positions. I think we need to finish the squad in maybe three, four positions, and then we have not to move too many players. We need to stay together. We need to improve the connection, the relationships, the style of play, quality of the play, the mentality, but we are in a good way to become better and do something special for this club.”

With Sávio ruled out for the remainder of 2026 and Spurs still searching for a clinical focal point up front alongside cover at full-back, De Zerbi’s comments signal targeted rather than wholesale recruitment in upcoming windows.

Having narrowly avoided relegation last season, Tottenham’s hierarchy invested heavily in reshaping the squad to suit De Zerbi’s football.

Spurs broke their club transfer record twice to sign midfielders Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes for a combined £185 million.

They also signed Jan Paul van Hecke for £52 million and Savio in a deal worth up to £85 million, while Omar Marmoush arrived on loan with a £60 million obligation to buy.

Experienced defenders Andy Robertson and Marcos Senesi were also brought in on free transfers, with established first-team players such as Cristian Romero and Djed Spence departing.

Although bedding in so many new faces contributed to a winless six-game opening stretch, those investments are now paying dividends.

Tottenham have now won four of their last five Premier League games, defeating Coventry City (3-1), Chelsea (2-0), Crystal Palace (2-0), and Ipswich Town (2-0).

The improved form has seen them go to 10th in the league table, with 15 points, just six points off fourth placed Liverpool.

With the January transfer window approaching, it will be interesting to see how many of those positions Tottenham attempt to strengthen midway through the season.

#1201. From young players to women's game to the national team, how can SFA duo Maxwell and Mulholland possibly be trusted to move things forward?

Published: 13:33 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 15:30 EST, 27 November 2026

With the Scottish FA’s widely trumpeted plan to get young players more game time now lying in a ditch off the M74, it was hard not to raise a wry smile at the midweek communique from Hampden over the intention to come up with some other kind of just-as-good idea somewhere in the new year.

‘Given the implications for our game, and our young talent, it is imperative that we take the necessary time to get those proposals right,’ it closed.

Bit late for that chat, is it not? Shouldn’t that work behind the scenes have been done before the grand summit at St Andrews back at the start of September when SFA chief executive Ian Maxwell and his chief football officer Craig Mulholland announced themselves lords and saviours of the national game with their scheme to shoehorn Under-21 players – no matter how good, bad or indifferent they may be – into club sides all over the country?

It all sounded good at the time, of course, if you put your head in the clouds and daydreamed over how pretty the world might be if everyone just got along.

Handwringers nationwide fell over themselves to simper the usual platitudes over how self-interest must be sacrificed for the greater good. There was probably some kind of online petition to link hands between all 42 senior grounds for a chorus of Kumbaya.

Meanwhile, anyone who has the faintest idea of the realpolitik of Scottish football looked at what was on the table and knew it was destined for the knacker’s yard.

SFA top brass Craig Mulholland and Ian Maxwell flank Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli

The SFA should have been consulting their more prominent clubs before going public over what might work and what might not, moulding something that the teams which matter were willing to support.

Instead, almost half the outfits in the Premiership blew their proposals out of the water in the end.

The sound of silence from Hampden, of course, had already become deafening as they realised they’d made a pig’s ear of it. Right now, it looks like everyone is back to the drawing board.

It’s embarrassing for the SFA. It has just made Maxwell and Mulholland look like they are incapable of taking the game with them on important matters.

Naturally, though, there wasn’t a single word from Haudit or Daudit in that press release to more or less confirm a major reverse ferret is going to be required. When things go belly-up, the high heid yins at Hampden are often nowhere to be seen.

Maxwell was too busy turning his mind to other matters during the week anyway, namely the fact that Scotland will be co-hosting the Women’s World Cup with the rest of the UK in 2035.

Given that was the only actual bid, the award of the event was hardly earth-shattering, but that didn’t stop Maxwell treating it as his Next Big Thing.

Maxwell has been in position at the SFA for more than eight years but has lacked real impact

‘I think it is going to be an absolutely transformational event to host in the UK and Ireland,’ he gushed. ‘The hard work starts now in terms of legacy and impact and driving everything we can from it.’

Hmmmm. Nice as it is that he’s managed to put being custard-pied at home by a large chunk of the Premiership over youth opportunities behind him, it might be wise to take Maxwell’s words over the women’s game with a pinch of salt.

He also called Scotland going to their first World Cup in 2019 ‘transformational’. Months later, Glasgow City won their 13th straight title with a ten-goal win over Motherwell on a council-run pitch in Wishaw in front of 100 people with no shelter, no seating and no obvious way for an ambulance to gain entry should a medical emergency occur. One Motherwell player had to nick across to the attached sports centre to get a chair for an injured team-mate to sit on.

A year had passed since the national team’s qualification, but there was still no kind of plan for the £400,000 prize money that they earned.

City’s Hayley Lauder, who’d been at the World Cup in France, tweeted: ‘Just won a league title in a public park at a sports centre. Not how I envisaged the game in 2019.’

It was a message that encapsulated the catastrophic failure to build on the incredible platform France 2019 provided under Maxwell’s reign.

Scotland celebrate an Erin Cuthbert goal against Argentina in 2019 before it all turned sour

That should have been the real launchpad for the women’s game here. Instead, it turned into a toxic shambles that killed any kind of momentum.

Progress since has been nothing like what it should have been. The national team, out to reach the next World Cup in next week’s play-off against Sweden, has been mired in failure. The women’s game lives back in the shadows amid pitiful attendances and an inability – or, it sometimes seems, refusal – to sell itself.

Yet, it could all have been so different. Just remember the scene back in ‘19. Scotland have to beat Argentina to make the last 16. A TV audience of six million watched the meeting with England earlier in the campaign.

The drama as Shelley Kerr’s side let slip a three-goal lead with 16 minutes to play – eventually drawing 3-3 thanks to a stoppage-time penalty retaken after an initial save by keeper Lee Gibson – was just incredible. It was the talk of the nation the next day.

And, then, it all just died a death. The head coach Shelley Kerr eventually coughed to the fact ‘a few drinks’ had been taken before a debrief the next day that reportedly left some players in tears.

No one wanted to talk about it. No one ever has, really. Yours truly asked Glasgow City for an interview with Gibson, then Alexander, in the early stages of the following season.

Top-flight matches between teams in the SWPL regularly take place on glorified public pitches

She’d been at the centre of a major global event. There was a story to be told. City insisted all requests had to be run past the SFA and their media office pretty much made it clear it wouldn’t be happening before she had even been asked.

No one told their stories of the biggest event in the history of women’s football here. Not properly. It felt like some kind of Omerta had been put in place over it.

Kerr, inexplicably, was allowed to keep her job by Maxwell and then failed to make it to Euro 2022. Instead, that year was marked by the women’s team, with Kerr gone, threatening to take legal action against the SFA over a lack of resources – with then captain Rachel Corsie referring to ‘years of iniquity, disrespect, and, in some cases, abuse.’

Yeah, the aftermath of France 2019 was ‘transformational’ all right. It transformed the hundreds of thousands of folk compelled to watch women’s football on national TV that summer back into people who forget it even exists.

Colleagues tell me there was no scope midweek to even interview anyone in a position of power within the SFA over what should have been a Good News Story regarding 2035. Hardly ‘driving everything we can from it’, is it?

I mean, how can you trust the likes of Maxwell to harness the opportunities afforded by that event – or Euro 2028 on home soil – when reflecting upon the raging binfire France 2019 became?

Mulholland is a regular sight being entertained by football matches up and down the country

How can you trust him and Mulholland to get it right on forging pathways for young players when they made such a Horlicks of trying to implement that poorly-planned proposal for Scotland-eligible Under-21s and failed again when changing it to involve Under-23s?

There’s a far wider issue with the production of players that involves going deep into the SFA’s own workings, addressing that lack of knowledge St Mirren boss Craig McLeish talked about at the lower levels of grassroots.

Indeed, there are problems all over the SFA. With refereeing standards. With VAR. With Steve Clarke admitting he forced the top brass into ‘panicking’ before the World Cup and giving him a new four-year deal.

If Maxwell and Mulholland’s blue-eyed boy Sebastien Pocognoli doesn’t start looking like he’s got a handle on his role as Clarke’s successor as national boss after a grim start to his reign, everything points to the two of them having to go the same way as their original Youth Plan. By being binned.

#1200. Genoa worry as Ostigard back in hospital after falling ill

Genoa are concerned for Norway international Leo Ostigard after he returned to hospital on his birthday, as the high fever and strong headaches have returned, while Lorenzo Colombo is out for the season with a torn ACL.

The defender was first taken to Genoa’s San Martino hospital late Monday night, as what at first appeared to be a regular flu turned more serious, with a high fever and severe headache.

After a couple of nights under observation, he was released on Wednesday and was expected to return to training with his teammates.

Instead, Primo Canale, Virgilio and more report that Ostigard was taken back into hospital on his 27th birthday and will undergo further neurological tests.

Meanwhile, Genoa striker Colombo has probably ended his season early, as he was diagnosed with a torn anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.

The Italian forward is set to undergo surgery and should be out for five to six months.

Midfielder Tommaso Baldanzi is suffering from a calf injury, so he too is out for this evening’s Serie A match against Inter.

#1199. A gut–brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Bidirectional communication between the brain and digestive tract is critical for optimizing nutrient preference and food intake, yet the neural mechanisms that couple gut nutrient sensing with ingestive motor control remain poorly understood. Here we identify a gut–brain sensory-motor circuit that regulates sugar ingestion in flies. We show that the brain neurons that regulate food ingestion, IN1s1, receive excitatory input from enteric sensory neurons that penetrate the foregut epithelium and detect sugars in the gut lumen during ingestion. Functional imaging and connectome analyses reveal that IN1s integrate excitatory input from multiple sugar-sensing neurons, including enteric sensory neurons, and provide inhibitory output to enteric motor neurons that control the muscles at the entry of the crop—a stomach-like organ. During ingestion, IN1 activation suppresses these enteric motor neurons, relaxes the crop duct and promotes rapid transfer of food into the crop, thereby enabling sustained food intake. Together, our findings describe a gut–brain circuit that controls the motor activity of digestive tract muscles during feeding and suggest a circuit mechanism by which nutrient signals from the gut contribute to the dynamic regulation of food intake across metabolic states.

Heatmaps show the synaptic distance (number of hops) from each neuron to each IN1; connections require ≥5 synapses. A threshold of 5 synapses is used to determine connectivity between pairs of neurons. f, EM reconstruction of putative IN1s (green) with different classes of PER neurons in the FAFB connectome (magenta, second-order PER; yellow, third-order PER; blue, pre-motor PER). IN1s are at least two synapses away from the PER-triggering second-order, third-order or motor neurons in the SEZ. A threshold of five synapses is used to determine connectivity between pairs of neurons. Anatomy of the top four postsynaptic outputs for IN1-1 (b), IN1-2 (d), IN1-3 (f), or IN1-4 (h) in the FAFB brain dataset is shown. The Codex IDs of output neurons and the percentage of synaptic outputs provided by IN1s are shown above each panel. A threshold of five synapses is used to determine connectivity between neurons. i, Summary of the synaptic connectivity of IN1s and their major outputs. Arrows indicate the direction of connections (from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurons). The six neurons (pink) shown in the bottom row (PRW.263, PRW.249, PRW.248, PRW.310, PRW.281, and PRW.274) are the crop-innervating enteric motor neurons (CEM neurons). Synaptic connections between IN1s are not shown in this graph. Illustrations are generated in the “Natverse” package in R (version 4.3.3) using data from FlyWire and the FAFB14 standard brain mesh.

a, IN1s are labelled by IN1>myr-GFP (green, left) and their putative postsynaptic partners revealed by trans-Tango (magenta) in the SEZ (middle) and crop duct (right) (scale bars = 50 μm). b, Representative confocal images of CEM neurons (green) in the male CNS (grey) and their descending projections towards the oesophagus (blue) (scale bars = 25 μm). c, CEM neurons (green) do not send projections to the VNC (grey) (scale bars = 25 μm). d, Confocal images of CEM neurons (green) in the female brain (grey) and their descending projections towards the oesophagus (blue) (scale bars = 25 μm). e, Synaptic terminals of CEM neurons (green) innervating the crop duct (blue) in a female fly. (scale bar = 25 μm). Supplementary Tables 1, 2 show full experimental genotypes and exact sample sizes. f, g, Schematic (generated in Adobe Illustrator) summarizing the proposed gut–brain circuit and its state-dependent regulation of crop filling. In both conditions, ingested sucrose passes through the foregut, and enteric Gr43a neurons (yellow) detect nutrient arrival in the gut and relay this signal to IN1s (green) in the brain (green arrow). IN1s integrate nutrient/taste input from multiple sources and inhibit CEM neurons (magenta; red lines), which in turn control the crop duct muscles to regulate the routing of ingested food into the crop. f, Under hungry, high-sugar-concentration conditions (~1 M sucrose), the IN1s drive sustained opening of the crop duct, resulting in high crop filling (orange dots indicate ingested sucrose). g, Under fed, low-sugar-concentration conditions (~100 mM sucrose), the same circuit produces only transient opening of the crop duct, resulting in low crop filling. Dashed arrows indicate the path of ingested food through the digestive tract. The differential crop-filling outcomes across conditions reflect the IN1 circuit’s integration of nutrient and metabolic-state information (VNC = ventral nerve cord). The fly schematic is adapted from a prior publication59.

#1198. Wesley Fofana’s Chelsea nightmare continues as Liverpool win shoot-out

Unfortunately for Chelsea, Wesley Fofana put his hand up twice. Firstly to concede the first-half penalty for handball that allowed Liverpool to equalise quickly after Chelsea themselves had scored from the spot.

And secondly to volunteer to take one of the penalties in the shoot-out. The defender had to score to keep Chelsea in it, but he woefully, nervously skied his effort high into a gleeful Kop and it was Liverpool who went through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.

LIVERPOOL ARE THROUGH TO THE QUARTER-FINALS OF THE CARABAO CUP! 🔴 Wesley Fofana blazes over to hand Liverpool their FIFTH consecutive victory ✅ https://t.co/M4n01R8DSk

There the reward for Andoni Iraola, the head coach, is a home tie against the club he left in the summer: Bournemouth. The draw has opened up for Liverpool, and they know it, with only Manchester City left of the other big guns. But despite again playing at Anfield, they would have preferred not to face such a dangerous and motivated opponent, who have just reeled off five wins and five clean sheets in a row under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose.

This was also a big win. A meaningful win. One that was celebrated as such with Dua Lipa’s One Kiss – an anthem on Jürgen Klopp’s run to Liverpool’s first Champions League final under him in 2018 – played over the loudspeakers at the end as the players joyfully milled around the pitch.

One kiss is all it takes 🎶 https://t.co/0jfujy4V94

“I am happy to feel it. We feel the support,” Iraola said when asked whether he sensed the momentum and togetherness building in his reshaped Liverpool side. It looks as though they are.

Fofana was Chelsea’s eighth taker, so they were running out of options, but it was a truly terrible effort. The 25-year-old turned and scratched his head – just as many Chelsea fans have done over his underwhelming, albeit injury-hit, contributions since his eyebrow-raising £75m move from Leicester City in 2022.

Both sides had the chance to win it earlier in the shoot-out. For Liverpool it was Kostas Tsimikas, who had taken the decisive kick to beat Chelsea in a shoot-out in the 2022 FA Cup final, but the Greek full-back also completely missed the target.

Tsimikas has the chance to put Liverpool through... And fires over the bar! 😱 https://t.co/eCKBT6njMB

Then Chelsea striker Emmanuel Emegha – on his debut – saw his kick saved, after an effort by Ryan Gravenberch had also been stopped. In the end, Liverpool’s stand-in captain Joe Gomez – still to score an actual goal – crashed in his kick before Fofana’s blunder. The 29-year-old Gomez finally “scored” and it was an assured strike.

This was the fifth penalty shoot-out between these two clubs, in all competitions, with Liverpool having now triumphed in all five. They won the toss for this one and elected to take the kicks in front of the Kop, which roared its satisfaction and did its best to unsettle the Chelsea takers.

Both stand-in goalkeepers – Giorgi Mamardashvili and Mike Penders – made one outstanding save each in the shoot-out. Chelsea substitute Valentín Barco was the other player to miss, hitting a post.

Chelsea blink first in the shootout! 🔵 Valentín Barco's penalty bounces off the post... https://t.co/rSXGfQctbI

The other efforts, in truth, were outstanding and assured with Liverpool, undoubtedly, benefitting from Iraola turning to his bench and bringing on Alexander Isak, Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. All scored their penalties.

Among Chelsea’s scorers was Jordan Henderson and the former Liverpool captain received a strange homecoming in his first appearance at Anfield for three years. He was booed, in the first half at least, and especially when he tucked the ball under his arm before Chelsea took their penalty – in normal time – which gave them the lead. Henderson turned to the stands, grinning.

Morgan Rogers buries the spotkick! ⚽️ Chelsea take the lead at Anfield 🔵 https://t.co/YlDn2gakRi

In truth it was more pantomime than meaningful and Henderson, like another former, Champions League-winning Liverpool midfielder Xabi Alonso – now Chelsea’s head coach – did not celebrate as Morgan Rogers scored. The penalty came after a rash challenge by Gravenberch, who crashed into Moisés Caicedo as the Chelsea captain ran on to Malo Gusto’s shrewd reverse pass inside the area.

Afterwards, Alonso faced more questions about his decision not to use Estêvão Willian. Despite injury to João Pedro and Cole Palmer’s suspension, there was only a place on the Chelsea bench for the 19-year-old Brazilian. And he stayed there even though Alonso used all five substitutions. Estêvão has made just two starts under Alonso, both in this competition. “The season is long and there will be moments for everyone,” Alonso said.

It was hardly a ringing endorsement especially as Alonso brought on Emegha instead. The 23-year-old striker’s contributions amounted to having his shoot-out penalty saved and then bizarrely and violently charging at Virgil van Dijk – his fellow Dutchman, is there an issue there? – long after the ball had gone, pushing the Liverpool captain over.

Virgil van Dijk was NOT HAPPY with Emmanuel Emegha 😒 https://t.co/UEtoJ7n5va

Alonso said the exit was a “small set-back,” and maybe it was, even if he started with a stronger side than Iraola. But with Chelsea not in European competition and unlikely to win the Premier League, it means he is already down to the FA Cup should silverware be won this season.

There is no VAR at this stage of the competition but referee Darren England appeared to get all the big calls right. Rogers claimed a penalty before Chelsea’s one was awarded, but Ronald Araújo was probably just too strong.

Morgan Rogers wants a penalty but he won't be getting one 🙅‍♂️ The referee waves it away and there's no VAR to step in... https://t.co/VR6yhBrx0I

More than two years have passed since Rio Ngumoha chose to leave Chelsea for Liverpool, but the frustration remains at Stamford Bridge. The pain of losing a player of Ngumoha’s potential does not pass quickly, especially as the winger was part of Chelsea’s academy system for eight years. It must sting to see a London boy, one of their own, now delighting the Anfield crowd.

For many at Chelsea, the anger at Ngumoha’s departure in 2024 will probably never subside. Or, at least, it will not subside while he continues to develop so thrillingly at Liverpool. Such was Chelsea’s annoyance at the time of his exit, Telegraph Sport reported last year, Liverpool’s scouts were subsequently banned from attending matches at their academy centre.

It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso said. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”

Former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

Tottenham winger Mykhailo Mudryk is currently expected to return to Chelsea at the end of the season despite Roberto De Zerbi remaining a huge admirer of the Ukrainian international, as per a report from Football Insider.

The 25-year-old joined Spurs in a surprise deadline-day loan move on September 1, with the agreement reportedly including a £75 million option to make the transfer permanent.

However, Mudryk has endured a frustrating spell in North London, with persistent injury problems preventing him from making an impression under De Zerbi.

The winger also recently angered sections of the Tottenham fanbase with his comments about wanting to join arch-rivals Arsenal.

Despite the controversy, De Zerbi remains keen to revive the career of a player he previously worked with at Shakhtar Donetsk.

Speaking on Football Insider’s Transfer Insider podcast, senior correspondent Pete O’Rourke revealed that Mudryk is currently expected to return to Chelsea once his loan agreement expires.

However, the journalist suggested that Tottenham could still consider a permanent move if De Zerbi manages to get the best out of the Ukrainian winger over the coming months.

“Look, he’s on loan at Tottenham until the end of the season, and then he’s expected to return to Chelsea.

“We know Roberto De Zerbi is a huge fan of Mudryk, having worked with him previously, and if he feels he can get the best out of Mudryk and he starts to show that he can get back to that player from a couple of seasons ago, then I’m sure Tottenham would be interested in signing him permanently, but we’re so far off that right now just because he’s had so few opportunities and so few minutes played so far.”

Also Read: Mykhailo Mudryk reveals he was handed pills on international duty in explosive doping claim

The primary obstacle preventing Mudryk from convincing Tottenham’s hierarchy to trigger a permanent deal has been persistent fitness misfortune.

Returning from a lengthy suspension over the summer, Mudryk made just one brief Premier League cameo, playing 17 minutes off the bench in a 0-0 draw away at Nottingham Forest on September 5, before sustaining a frustrating non-contact ankle injury in training.

That setback has kept him sidelined throughout autumn, leaving him with zero goals, zero assists, and zero shots in a Tottenham shirt.

With Savio also ruled out for the rest of 2026, De Zerbi hopes Mudryk can finally return in December to salvage his loan stint.

#1196. Hutchinson stars against Forest owner’s Olympiacos, but Milan still face 50m decision

Omari Hutchinson scored one goal and provided two assists in Milan’s 4-2 win over Olympiacos mid-week, but the Rossoneri still need Nottingham Forest to lower their demands for a potential permanent transfer over the summer.

The versatile 23-year-old was the undisputed Man of the Match in Milan’s 4-2 Europa League win over Olympiacos on Thursday, scoring one goal and providing two assists.

Without a doubt, that was his best performance in a Milan shirt so far and, as Gazzetta reported, the Rossoneri will need more games at that level from him to activate a €50m clause and sign him permanently next summer.

Hutchinson is on loan at San Siro from Nottingham Forest, but the fee agreed with the Premier League side last summer is still too high for the Rossoneri.

Gazzetta reports that the Serie A giants are very open to retaining Hutchinson at San Siro, although a single good performance still isn’t enough to trigger such a high clause. This means that if the 23-year-old doesn’t show consistency, the Rossoneri will consider a permanent transfer only for a lower fee.

Ironically, Hutchinson’s best Milan performance so far came against Olympiacos, the Greek club owned by Evangelos Marinakis, who has a majority stake in Nottingham Forest.

Hutchinson still isn’t a regular starter under Ruben Amorim, but has full trust from the Portuguese coach and Milan owner Gerry Cardinale.

Hutchinson has already made it clear he’d like to stay at Milan long-term, but whether that happens depends on his performances in the coming months.

Hutchinson has scored two goals and provided three assists in 14 appearances across all competitions, but has only started twice in Serie A.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

He was great on Thursday, but he needs to do that at least 10 or 15 times during the rest of the season if Milan are going to pay £50m.

#1195. Farm that became a football factory: Club where Man United, Liverpool, Man City, Leeds and Ireland legends started out is back in national Cup final... and hoping it's the first of many more glory days

Published: 16:16 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 16:26 EST, 27 November 2026

Gavin Whelan had been away from the domestic game for a while and hadn’t really been looking for a way back in.

The former Drogheda United and Bray Wanderers player had stepped away from the League of Ireland at 29 and his involvement in football in the past few years had been restricted to helping coach his older son Jayden’s team as they went through the age grades at Home Farm – the fourth generation of the Whelan family to come through the club.

The Whelan dynasty, with Gavin second from right beside his uncle Ronnie (centre) and Paul (seond from left)

But when it emerged the FAI were setting up a third tier, he had a chat with Brian Honohan, who had been a Shamrock Rovers teammate of his father, Paul, and they decided to put together a group that would help put Home Farm back where they belong.

This inaugural National League final in Carlisle Grounds is a step in that direction. Home Farm face Lucan United, who beat them 2-0 in Whitehall recently in the group stages. In a way, it is like the old meeting the new although the fact that two Dublin clubs are contesting the first final in a concept that was supposed to broaden the league’s base to uncharted territories will be viewed a little sceptically.

But that shouldn’t take away from what both Home Farm and Lucan are trying to do – or the sense of camaraderie and purpose that has characterised the first truncated season of the third tier.

Clubs have become comrades in what they are trying to do – right down to ensuring each visiting team would sit down for a meal after the final whistle before beginning the journey home.

‘There has been a sense that we all have to help each other, that we are all in this together,’ says Home Farm chairman Brendan Menton.

‘So, the clubs would organise something to eat for the visiting team. It meant that if Bonagee had to go back up the road to Donegal, they wouldn’t need to stop off somewhere. It was a small thing, but it has built a real sense of togetherness among all 15 clubs.’

Nicola Brannigan (second from left), Brendan Menton (centre), Richard Dunne (second right) and Gavin Peers (right)

Brendan Menton senior was one of the founders of Home Farm back in 1928

Menton is a former chief executive of the FAI, holding that position during Saipan in 2002. But his footballing roots have been in Home Farm.

Like Whelan, Menton’s family have four generations who have lined out for the famous nursery – with his two grandchildren currently part of the underage teams. And his father, Brendan senior, was one of the founding members of the club back in 1928.

The club came into existence when Leo Fitzmaurice, concerned about the lack of recreational facilities for young people in the Drumcondra and Whitehall area, decided to set up a street league.

Home Farm Road, which is a street in the locality, was one of the roads that formed a team.

‘My father was one of the founding members of the club, who were established to play in the Drumcondra and Whitehall street league. My family lived on 31 Home Farm Road, the name came from a Monastery that was on Iona Road and back a few centuries ago, every Monastery had their own home farm and that’s where the name came from.

‘The story goes that one Friday evening, some boys from the Richmond Road team, which included Don Seery, came to play Home Farm Road but their ball burst so the two teams decided to amalgamate and from that, the club was born.’

And from such uncertain beginnings grew one of the most successful schoolboy clubs in Ireland. More than 50 Irish internationals have passed through its famous nursery – from Jackie Carey and Liam Whelan to Gary Kelly and Richard Dunne.

One of the club’s greatest claims to fame was that in the opening game of the 2023 women’s World Cup, two former Home Farm players were on the pitch, one for Ireland and one for Australia – in Abbie Larkin and Mary Fowler, who grew up for a few years in Dublin.

Ireland legends Dunne, Gary Kelly in his Leeds days and inset Jackie Carey, who captained Manchester United

While it was a schoolboy club nurturing young talent that Home Farm fostered its reputation, it was elected to the League of Ireland in 1972 and three years later achieved its greatest ever success as, in an underdog story to rival Leicester winning the Premier League, they won the FAI Cup.

Menton can still list off the names of all the players for the club’s most famous day in April 1975, including a young Dermot Keely who was in the centre of defence, and Martin Murray, who at 16 was the youngest player to win a FAI Cup medal.

‘Everyone but Jack Dempsey, who was in his late 20s or 30 at the time, was 24 years of age or under. The average age of the team was just 21 and a lot of the players were younger than that, it was an incredible achievement at the time,’ he says.

It is that sort of rich and illustrious history that Whelan, Honohan and the other stakeholders want to tap into when they were looking for a pathway back into the league. Home Farm, who had an association with Everton in the latter part of the 1990s, dropped out of the league in 1999 with the franchise being taken up by Dublin City who were eventually subsumed into Sporting Fingal, both now sadly defunct.

The Everton connection came through Martin Murray and saw one of the later graduates of the schoolboy club, Richard Dunne, whose uncle Theo was a coach at Home Farm, go over to Goodison Park as a teenager.

‘I played my schoolboy football at Home Farm and got picked up to go to Everton at 15,’ Dunne remembers.

‘We didn’t have the pathway produced by the National League then. And Home Farm was considered the top schoolboy club in Dublin at the time and when scouts and English clubs came over, this was the first port of call. That’s something that probably faded away over time, but hopefully, we can get it back.’

Team captain Jack Dempsey lifted the FAI Cup for Home Farm back in 1975

There are around 30 teams at the club now, 10 of them in an underage girls section. The hope is that the likes of Larkin and Fowler can be an inspiration for the next generation.

The club will also move to a new facility in the AUL next summer, as part of the deal that was made when the construction of the Metrolink means that they have to relocate temporarily from their nursery’s home on Mobhi Road in Glasnevin.

They have also got a tie-in with neighbouring Dublin City University, links that the club will hope to deepen. The third-level institution is seen more as a GAA university, but the hope is that they can develop a soccer scholarship programme, so players from the north of the city don’t have to travel to UCD or Shamrock Rovers.

Whelan, who availed of the UCD scholarship, says it is still in the early stages, but it is one aspect that reveals the ambitions of the club.

Nicola Brannigan, who formerly worked in the FAI marketing department but is now chief executive of the club, says the relationship has developed through the inaugural season in the national league.

‘We have students from DCU doing work experience at the club, we have communications students coming in to help us with social media, there is a law student from DCU, so that is one way that the relationship has worked. And then we have a few students or DCU graduates playing for the team,’ she says.

Under former Sligo Rovers star Gavin Peers, who played with the club as a youngster, the senior team have performed above themselves at times this season, but the ambitions are such they always felt they would be in contention to win the inaugural National League.

But the season has more being about putting Home Farm back on the map. Whelan knows from personal experience what can happen when clubs in the league endure harsh times.

Having scored in the FAI Cup final for Drogheda and winning a league title with them, he was there when things went awry a couple of years later.

Home Farm have not beaten Lucan United so far this season

‘There was a lot of good people in Drogheda at the time, but it is what can happen when the economy goes south for a club and that is why what we want to build here, we want to do in a conservative and sustainable way and it is why we made sure that the senior club, and the club that we want to eventually get back in the Premier Division, is separate from the schoolboy section.’

Whelan’s youngest son Sonny is now playing at the under-eight team, the second in a fourth generation of Whelans to pass through Home Farm, stretching back to Whelan’s father Paul and uncle Ronnie and his grandfather, Ronnie senior.

But a greater claim to fame was that Whelan’s goal for Drogheda in 2005 meant that he, his father Paul, who won it with Bohemians, and his grandfather Ronnie senior were the first three generations of the same family  to win a national cup in a European league.

But it all started in Home Farm, which is why he wants to bring the club back to the big-time, especially with the club's centenary coming up in 2028.

‘We want to bring back Home Farm, by using the foundations of what made the club in the past, and its rich history,’ he says.

‘This is where I learned manners, learned discipline, learned teamwork and all of that. The club always had the right ethos and this was just a case of leaving a legacy, showing what the club is and leaving it in a better place.’

Even though there is no promotion into the First Division this season, it feels like winning the inaugural National League will serve notice of the club’s intention of returning to where they feel they belong.

Crystal Palace manager Thomas Frank has urged Yeremy Pino to improve his disciplinary record after the Spanish attacker picked up another suspension ahead of Sunday’s crucial Premier League clash against Hull City.

The 24-year-old has emerged as one of Palace’s standout performers during an otherwise disappointing campaign, but his mounting yellow card tally has become a growing concern.

Pino picked up his fifth Premier League booking of the season during last weekend’s 3-2 defeat against Coventry City, ruling him out of Sunday’s encounter.

The Spaniard was cautioned again during Thursday’s 2-1 Europa League victory over 10-man Real Sociedad, receiving his fourth European booking of the campaign and incurring another suspension.

Speaking during his pre-match press conference ahead of the Hull City clash, Frank acknowledged Pino’s importance to Crystal Palace while insisting that the winger needs to address his disciplinary problems.

The Danish manager said (via The Standard): “Yes, I think it’s fair to say. I think he’s a very good player , very important for us and has gone up a level this season, so of course it is disappointing.

“Yes, I think it’s fair to say. I think he’s a very good player — very important for us and has gone up a level this season — so of course it is disappointing.

“It is something he needs to work on. That is too many yellow cards. Of course, we would have loved to play with Yeremy and [Ismaïla] Sarr and JP [Jean-Philippe Mateta] in an important match — three of our best offensive players — but others will need to step up and show what they can do.”

Appointed earlier this month on a two-and-a-half-year contract following Pierre Sage’s dismissal, Frank faces an uphill battle to keep the Eagles in the top flight.

Palace currently sit bottom of the Premier League table with the division’s leakiest defense, having conceded 24 goals across their opening 10 matches.

Frank suffered a disappointing 3-2 defeat against Coventry City in his first game in charge before securing a morale-boosting first victory against Real Sociedad on Thursday.

The Danish manager will now be hoping to carry that momentum into the Premier League as Palace look to climb out of the relegation zone.

While improving Palace’s defensive record will undoubtedly be among Frank’s biggest priorities, keeping his most influential attacking players available will be equally important.

Manchester United are among the favourites to land Nico Paz, however there is one big obstacle standing in the way of a blockbuster move to Old Trafford.

According to The Athletic, Manchester United have placed the 22-year-old Como sensation high on their shortlist of potential replacements should captain Bruno Fernandes depart Old Trafford next summer.

Although Real Madrid hold an €80 million buy-back clause for summer 2027 after selling him permanently to Como for €60 million last summer, Paz is currently reluctant to return to the Bernabéu without guaranteed starter minutes, opening the door for Como to sell him on the open market.

However, as per the report, there is one decisive hurdle: Champions League qualification.

While United’s long-term project and global stature appeal to the Argentina international, Old Trafford may not be his first choice unless Mauricio Pochettino can guide the club back into Europe’s premier competition.

Arsenal have also initiated contact, intensifying competition for his signature.

Speaking on his YouTube channel, transfer expert Fabrizio Romano confirmed United’s strong admiration for Paz, revealing that club chiefs were blown away when he registered two goals and an assist in Como’s 4-1 Champions League demolition of United in October:

“Manchester United are following Nico Paz closely. They were falling in love with Nico Paz when he played against them in Como.”

One major factor handing United a crucial edge in negotiations is representation.

Romano further revealed that Paz is represented by the exact same agency as compatriot and United manager Mauricio Pochettino, giving the Red Devils a direct line to the player’s camp ahead of a fiercely contested summer race.

With uncertainty continuing to surround Fernandes’ long-term future at Old Trafford, identifying a potential successor appears to be among United’s recruitment priorities.

The Portuguese international has reportedly rejected two contract offers from United, with his existing agreement running until the summer of 2027, although the club retain an option to extend it by a further year.

Replacing Fernandes’ creativity, goalscoring ability and influence in the final third would be an enormous challenge.

At just 22, the Argentine would also represent a significant investment in the future as Pochettino looks to rebuild the squad.

The prospect of working under his compatriot could appeal to Paz, but United may first need to prove they can offer him the platform to compete at the highest level of European football.

#1191. Martin O'Neill's team selections in Europa League say it all about Celtic's glaring lack of ambition

Published: 13:07 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 16:44 EST, 27 November 2026

Ross Desmond started it at last season’s comedy turn of a Celtic AGM when more or less admitting that finances mean it’s time to run up the white flag when trying to compete in Europe.

And manager Martin O’Neill’s team selections in this term’s Europa League only heighten the concern that addressing a truly horrific record in UEFA competition dating back two decades now is not a priority.

It is a desperate situation for the club to be in. O’Neill might talk about rotation or private masterplans over impact substitutions, but it is seriously wrong that Camilo Duran, for example, was left on the bench for the recent meetings with Besiktas and Torreense.

Duran, himself, proved it by coming on and scoring the goals that mean qualification for the knockout rounds remains a distinct possibility despite everything.

It just looks like the club and its manager don’t really care all that much about Europe – or don’t see it as a key priority – and that’s not acceptable when they have charged their punters big-money for packages to get into the ground to watch it.

There are a number of things that need addressed when this year’s AGM rolls back around next Tuesday, though, and it is to be hoped punters and shareholders – probably the same thing, really – have prepared with cooler heads this time round.

Celtic line up for their tie against Torreense, with star man Camilo Duran again left on the bench

Last year became embarrassing, really, with people holding up red cards, jeering, walking out and chanting ‘Sack The Board’. They gave those at the top table the opportunity to bring the meeting to a halt and that’s exactly what happened before they had been properly challenged.

That behaviour is OK when making a point inside the stadium on matchday. If you want to win an argument – or unpick one – inside a business meeting, though, the shouting has to be replaced with clear thinking, planning and strong cases delivered in a coherent manner.

There are so many things to tear into CEO Michael Nicholson and co over. There’s the evident lack of long-term planning that has a 74-year-old in O’Neill still in charge of running the team.

There’s recruitment, in the week of a tie-up with little-known Pluto Data Analytics. Celtic went into their Champions League play-off with LASK Linz unprepared and suffered humiliation. Their dealings at the end of the summer window were erratic and scattergun.

Even marquee signings Kasper Hogh and Haissem Hassan are unravelling. They look like two guys totally unsuited to the way O’Neill wants to play and speak to a disjointed, failing policy.

There has been no full-time chairman appointed to replace 77-year-old interim Brian Wilson. There’s no sporting director or head of football operations. No one seems to want to explain who exactly will be working with Pluto to try and improve the club’s record on signings.

Martin O'Neill and assistant Shaun Maloney watch as Celtic toil against Torreense in Leiria

Parkhead’s now old and outdated. Millions lie around in the bank for no particular reason. Communication between the board and a disgruntled fanbase needs improved dramatically.

There is a lot to get through next week. That’s why there can be no place for student politics, silly protests, angry chanting. This board needs taken to task and it is to be hoped there are fans ready to step up to the mic and confront them calmly.

Celtic regard themselves as one of the biggest clubs in the world. This apparent insouciance over Europe is at complete odds with that, though.

It is as clear a sign as any that standards have slipped so badly at the champions and it is something that needs to be called out and challenged in the right way.

#1190. Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

The lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the issues Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N

The last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

“We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

What they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

James Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU

The roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI

It must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

The whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

#1189. Fabregas: ‘Nico Paz a wonderful cocktail, Como players want Man City and Juventus’

Cesc Fabregas hailed Nico Paz as ‘a wonderful cocktail’ of a football player, as the coach admits young players ‘don’t see Como as the apex of their careers, they want Manchester City or Juventus.’

The 22-year-old was a product of the Real Madrid youth academy and has flourished during his co-ownership deal with Como.

That saw the Serie A club pay €60m to buy the other 50 per cent over the summer, giving Real Madrid an option to purchase him in June 2027 for €80m.

“Nico is physique and talent, vision and mentality,” said Fabregas in a press conference today.

“He is a wonderful cocktail, his Mum and Dad did a great job. I used to play in his position, so I like talking to him, find out if he sees the same things I do. At times, I think players don’t even need to be coached on movement or control, it’s more about tactics.

“The great thing about Nico Paz is he doesn’t think about it, he just does the right things.”

There have been strong reports of a potential bidding war for Nico Paz in the summer, including Arsenal, Manchester United and more.

Fabregas took the opportunity to muse on modern coaching methods and whether there is the risk of limiting the talent at the disposal of players.

“Nowadays, we risk creating robots, which helps a certain type of player. However, with Nico Paz, knowing he can make the right choice to win or make the difference, that really helps.

“This not thanks to my work. We just tried to push him on his mentality and consistency, but having a Number 10 that defends like he does, or a Number 9 like Tasos Douvikas who can help the defence, that’s special.

“We are very happy with Nico Paz, and the credit all belongs to him.”

Fabregas has been able to develop many young players in his Como squad, who would’ve struggled for playing time elsewhere.

Instead, they are featuring regularly in Serie A and the Champions League, gaining valuable experience.

“A young player is like a sponge, he soaks up knowledge,” added the coach.

“Como is not the apex of their career, they want to go to Manchester City or Juventus. They listen, always want to find space, are very intuitive and ask lots of questions.

“We have here a serious, professional attitude, even when the players are young. When they are ready to take flight and Como is no longer in their plans, is the moment they will be allowed to fly away, and we will sign someone else.”
