#1183. Serie A | Frosinone 3-0 Parma: Bobcek hat-trick hero in first start

Tomas Bobcek marked his first Serie A start with a hat-trick, as Frosinone registered a sixth straight home victory to crush Parma 3-0.

The Canarini saw their excellent start to the season stall with back-to-back defeats against Cagliari and Milan. Antonio Raimondo was surprisingly back on the bench after nearly a month out, but Daniel Birligea replaced him on the treatment table, so Tomas Bobcek got his first start. Parma also lost two on the bounce, with Lautaro Valenti suspended, David Romero and Dominik Drobnic injured.

The first real save came after 21 minutes, with Giorgi Kvernadze on the counter-attack to sting Giovanni Daffara’s gloves, the Patrizio Masini follow-up much easier to deal with.

Ilario Monterisi was decisive at the other end moments later, performing a goal-line clearance on the Nesta Elphege prod from a Parma corner.

Bobcek’s acrobatic overhead kick landed on the roof of the net from a Fares Ghedjemis cross, and Monterisi nodded the Giacomo Calò corner over the bar, but El Bilal Touré fired wide after catching Calvani napping.

Calò drilled just wide from the edge of the area, then after the restart a similar Romano Schmid effort forced the Daffara save at the far bottom corner.

Frosinone finally found the breakthrough when Ghedjemis controlled the Calò cross-field pass and stung Daffara’s gloves at the near post, but Bobcek was quickest to react on the rebound, marking his first Serie A start with his debut goal.

It was nearly a second moments later, Daffara parrying the Bobcek header on a corner, and the brace was completed with his acrobatic volley on the Masini cross from the right.

Bobcek made it a hat-trick, running onto the Alessio Zerbin through ball and beating the on-rushing goalkeeper from close range.

Parma’s best opportunity came in added time, the El Bilal Touré scorcher smashing against the crossbar.

#1182. Jamie Vardy’s Wife Responds to Striker Missing Burnley Match to Watch Leicester

Jamie Vardy wasn't included in Burnley's squad for their visit to Millwall on Saturday afternoon, and the player's wife has now provided some clarity on this absence.

The Clarets currently sit in a perilous position inside the Championship's bottom three, and thus, the trip to fellow strugglers Millwall is a hugely important clash in Fabio Celestini's side's season. Despite this, Vardy has been allowed to miss the away day entirely for a very unconventional reason.

The legendary Leicester City striker signed for the Lancashire outfit in the summer on a free transfer, after parting ways with Italian side Cremonese at the end of last season.

Scoring just one goal since his switch to Turf Moor, the 39-year-old has found it difficult to help guide Burnley away from the relegation zone in his limited minutes.

Burnley are winless in their last eight matches and have claimed just one victory all season in the Championship. Every game is crucial for the Clarets in their bid for survival, yet Celestini told Vardy he wasn't needed for Saturday's encounter with Millwall.

The second-tier side travelled to the Den without their veteran centre-forward because the ex-Halifax Town man is attending his former club Leicester's match against Mansfield Town in League One with his family.

According to talkSPORT, Vardy made himself available for the game in South London, explicitly not requesting the weekend off, but Celestini notified the player that he wasn't required, essentially permitting his absence.

Vardy's wife and children had already planned to travel to the East Midlands to watch the match at the King Power Stadium on Saturday afternoon, so the number nine has decided to join them as a result of his head coach's decision.

Unsurprisingly, some fans took Vardy's exclusion from the squad for the Millwall fixture at face value, criticising the player for seemingly prioritising attending a Leicester match over playing for the club that employs him.

However, Rebekah Vardy rubbished this idea, replying to an Instagram post from a Burnley supporter that threw this criticism at the striker.

"Not true, just told not needed!" she wrote.

West Ham, Wrexham, and Blackburn Rovers have all been predicted for huge seasons, but each have different fates in next season's Championship.

It marked the fourth game running in which Vardy hasn't been named in Celestini's starting eleven. The experienced forward has very much found himself in a peripheral role at Turf Moor, with Zeki Amdouni usurping him in the pecking order in recent weeks.

Burnley will hope that Vardy can rediscover the prolific form he's shown throughout his distinguished career, as they look to preserve their 26-year-long status as a top-two-division club.

#1181. Man Utd 0-4 Brentford: Patrick Dorgu Labelled ‘Top 3 Worst Signing Ever’

A Manchester derby in the Championship is becoming a real possibility after Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United fell to an embarrassing 4-0 defeat to Brentford. Fans have now questioned his decision over one of his struggling players.

United started fairly well but were wasteful in front of goal, and the visitors made them pay in the 19th minute. Callum Wilson pounced to fire past Senne Lammens, and Pochettino's players' heads dropped after a promising start.

Wilson was at it again in the 32nd minute. This time, more calamitous defending from the hosts allowed the English striker to fire under Lammens. The Belgian goalkeeper perhaps should have done better but could do nothing about Kristoffer Ajer's 82nd finish.

It proved to be a nightmare debut for Pochettino at the supposed Theatre of Dreams. Kevin Schade's 90+2nd minute goal compounded his woes and handed him a second consecutive 4-0 league loss.

Pochettino made some bold decisions when naming his team, including in attack. He opted to start Amad Diallo, Joshua Zirkzee, and Patrick Dorgu in a three-man frontline, leaving Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo on the bench which was a surprise given how important they were last season.

The Argentine persisted with the trio despite them collectively scoring just four goals between them since January. They never looked like getting on the scoresheet today, and their lack of threat was on full display.

Dorgu, in particular, put in a disappointing performance, wasting a golden opportunity before Wilson's opener. A ball into the box found the Danish winger at the back post, but with the goal gaping, he headed wide.

Paul Merson couldn't believe what he was seeing while covering the game on Sky Sports: "Dorgu has missed a sitter. If he hits the target, he can't help but score."

Dorgu missed another decent chance in the second half when played through by Bruno Fernandes. His left-footed strike could only find the gloves of Caoimhín Kelleher, much to his captain's frustration.

Dorgu is a versatile player, able to play on the right or left wing as well as at left wing-back. He arrived during Ruben Amorim's tenure, and the Portuguese coach initially viewed him as a wing-back before eventually deploying him as a winger.

The 22-year-old arrived at Old Trafford from Lecce in January 2025 in a £30 million deal. He has since made 58 appearances, scoring five goals and providing eight assists.

Pochettino's decision to start Dorgu over Cunha didn't go down well with much of the United fanbase. Supporters feel the Brazilian, who finished last season with 10 goals in 33 league games, should be starting with the club sitting 19th in the table.

One fan made their feelings clear with a post on X: "Dorgu left wing experiment should have been over from the carrick days Cunha is right there bro."

Another supporter agreed with this verdict: "I think this should be the last time Cunha gets benched for Patrick Dorgu."

Other fans were more focused on Dorgu's long-term place in the squad, with one offering a brutal assessment: "Dorgu top 3 worst utd signings ever alongside mount and Donny van de beek."

Another argued: "I just don’t see how Dorgu has a future at United."

One fan admitted they were unsure what Dorgu brings to the side: "I don’t understand Dorgu. When he plays LB, he doesn’t want to defend, and wants to play up high like a winger. You play him as a winger, he refuses to take his man on and take his chances in the box. I get RW is his best position, but still— horror footballer."

Another agreed: "For a guy where PnP is his selling point, Dorgu doesn’t play or run with any intensity."

If Crystal Palace beat Hull City at home on Sunday, United will enter December bottom of the Premier League. Pochettino has been tasked with turning the situation around, but without a win in his opening three games, his side finds themselves as the biggest club in a relegation battle in Premier League history.

Mauricio Pochettino will be desperate to add a new left-back to his Manchester United squad when the January transfer window opens

Starting Dorgu over Cunha, given their respective contributions at the club, doesn't help, nor does statistically the worst defence in Europe's top five leagues. It will be interesting to see what the higher-ups decide to do in January and whether they embark on the busiest winter transfer window in club history.

#1180. He's savoured silverware, snubbed the 49ers and set Derek McInnes on the path to managerial success... but all former St Johnstone chairman Geoff Brown wanted was to make the people of Perth proud

Published: 17:30 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 17:32 EST, 27 November 2026

The child is the father to many traits that inhabit the man.

Geoff Brown walked into his home more than 70 years ago to a mother crying because she feared she could not put bread on the table. Now, at 83, he knows that his children, grandchildren and great grandchildren will never suffer that anguish.

He was a child who lived in a cramped house with the family of eight at one time sharing three rooms. He made his business by building large family homes and constructing a huge one for himself.

He was a football player and coach in his childhood and as a young adult. He then bought a football team as a successful businessman and his unflinching tenure ensured it would survive and then prosper. He was born in St Johnstouns Nursing Home in 1943 and later would own St Johnstone.

As a child, too, he had a working horse, Prince. As a multimillionaire, he had a string of racehorses. He now focuses on providing horses and hosting events for Riding for the Disabled.

The foundations of his future were laid in his childhood.

Geoff Brown was chairman at St Johnstone for 38 years and retains a deep bond with the club

The most public achievement is his stewardship of St Johnstone. The club, simply, would not be still playing if Brown had not stepped in and run it for 38 years.

‘If I knew then what I later knew then I would never have got involved,’ he says briskly of his takeover in 1986. ‘No one would have touched St Johnstone with a bargepole.’

Brown, then, has lived a full life but its broad scope can shimmer with odd, illuminating moments. His conversation is serious but never dull. He tells of how the mobile phone bill of Derek McInnes was evidence he was an excellent manager, how his grandmother was his driving force, and how football made him indulgent without measure.

He sets out his philosophy in simple terms. The son of a struggling market gardener, he says: ‘People are what matter. All my life I have wanted to provide for my family.’

The Browns, with six children, lived in a house with no bathroom. There were two bedrooms for the children. The parents slept in the living room.

‘Even today, at the age of 83, I have a vivid memory of being 10 years old and seeing my mother in tears because we didn’t have money for bread.’

Brown and his son Steve, who took over as chairman, celebrate double cup success in 2021

The teenage Brown left school, became a joiner, started a business and built a portfolio of interests that all stemmed from his hard work and ability to make a deal.

He insists his greatest skills are ‘to be observant and have commonsense’. The first trait is exemplified by his aside when assessing his former manager, McInnes.

‘His phone bill during the summer was twice as much as any other manager we ever had,’ he says.

‘What does that tell you? Yes, he was working away trying to get players in and seeing what was going on. He never stopped.

‘Football is gossip. If you know what is going on then you are a step ahead. Derek was ready on day one of the season.’

Paul Sturrock, a firm friend, remains his favourite Saints manager but his appraisal of McInnes is stunning. Asked about the task at Rangers, he says: ‘I don’t see another manager in Scotland who could do the job he will do. He has a positive mindset. He makes decisions and then gets on with it.’

There is more than a bit of that in Brown’s personality. ‘Yes, I never had five-year plans or any ultimate strategy,’ he says. ‘I just get up in the morning and deal with what is in front of me.’

Brown is full of admiration for the managerial talents of Derek McInnes, whom he hired in 2007

This energy took him to St Johnstone. He made it clear from his first interest in the club that he was not going to be a collegiate manager. Brown was going to run it his way. ‘There was no way I was going to become involved unless I had complete control,’ he writes in his autobiography.

The club’s substantial debts emerged quickly. ‘I hadn’t seen the books and the directors hadn’t told me how bad things were. It soon became clear what a mess the club was in financially.’

He wrote a cheque for £100,000 immediately. ‘Aye, if I knew then what I know now…’

His decades at the helm of St Johnstone, in bad times and in glorious moments, have given him stark lessons. ‘With football it is money, money, money,’ he says.

The commonsense, he admits, was an early casualty. He had promised the players a communal bonus of £250,000 if they finished fourth and gained European competition in the 1998/99 season.

‘They then asked for £500,000 if they finished third and I said: “Okay, they will never do that”. Of course, they did and then we made nothing near that in Europe.’

Brown looks out over the club's old Muirton Park home before the move to McDiarmid Park

In the qualifying round for the UEFA Cup, the Saints beat Finnish side VOS but were beaten in the first round proper by Monaco.

‘I felt I was too soft in football,’ says Brown, ‘As I say, it was all about money and people can get swept along.’

He sidesteps any praise for the Scottish Cup win in 2014 and the domestic cup double in 2021, pointing out they occurred under the reign of his son, Steve. He pays tribute, too, to Stewart Duff, who was a stalwart as managing director in those times.

Yet Brown was a constant presence and a huge influence at the club until he sold it to Adam Webb in 2024. The deal was done on a handshake and Brown later learned that the 49ers group, who subsequently took over Rangers, were keen to talk. ‘There were no discussions,’ he says. ‘I shook Adam’s hand and a deal is a deal. I would not have talks with anyone else once I had given my word.’

He adds: ‘One thing is odd, though. Adam had to give up his share in Cambridge before the SFA would allow him to progress with the deal. Yet the 49ers still have a share in Leeds.’

He worries about Scottish football. ‘It’s difficult for clubs. They are all in tough positions,’ he says. This is primarily in reference to finances but he has deep concerns about the dearth of young players coming through.

Brown with new club chairman and owner Adam Webb, who bought the Perth outfit in 2024

Asked what he would do first if he was at the Scottish Football Association, he answers quickly: ‘I would reintroduce primary school football. That is where all the great players learned. I ran an under-13 team at St Madoes and that was the progression for primary schools.

‘The club academies have not worked. Players are rejected too early and for the wrong reasons. Someone who is small at ten can be tall at 15. Players progress at different rates and once there was that path from school to boys’ club to Juniors or above.’

The problem is visible. ‘I watched three games recently: Switzerland v Scotland, Wales v Portugal and Motherwell v Rangers. Wales were much better than us, good to watch. In the Motherwell game, there was not a single Scottish player on the park,’ he says.

He has other interests to comfort him. He is a keen golfer and does a bit of shooting. He also has retained his interest in horses. He no longer has thoroughbreds in training but has devoted time and money for disabled people, particularly children, having a place to ride horses.

In 2014, he created a charity and refurbished a large barn at Castle Farm, Kinfauns, to be fully compliant with the needs of Riding For the Disabled.

Brown proudly shows the Princess Royal around his Kinfauns stable in Perthshire in 2016

He and his family never took a wage out of St Johnstone. The money for the riding at Castle Farm is generated by Brown. The horses are his.

So what was his reward for decades in sport? Was it the joy of being in control at a football club?

‘No, that was a bit of a bind, to be honest. It took far more time out of my life than I ever thought,’ he says.

But surely providing pleasure to generations of Saints fans, giving them days of glory in finals and seeing them play in Europe, that must mean something?

‘The thing I have always wanted was to give something back to the people of Perthshire,’ he says. But he does not expand.

Horses have played a central role in Brown life and he helps run Riding for the Disabled charity

In the book there is a poignant scene of Brown watching a disabled girl being helped from a horse back into her wheelchair.

‘Aye, I always remember her smile,’ he says to me. ‘That is payment in full.’

Geoff Brown: always observant but blessed with more than commonsense.

■ Building My Life: The Geoff Brown Story is published by GS Brown Consulting. All profits will go to Saints in the Community

#1179. 5 Best Free Agent Strikers Man Utd Can Sign Now as They Feel Benjamin Sesko's Absence

James is a Senior Editor for GIVEMESPORT with over eight years of experience in the industry. After graduating from the University of Southampton in 2016 with a degree in history, he joined the company as an Academy member in July 2017 and, after a short time working as a freelancer, was given a full-time role in February 2018.  He primarily covers the biggest stories in the football world but is also comfortable reporting on a variety of other sports including darts, golf, Formula 1, tennis, boxing and athletics. He has covered some massive events during his time at GIVEMESPORT, including numerous Champions League and World Cup finals, as well as the Olympics in 2020 and 2024.

Manchester United have had a dismal start to the 2026/27 season, and a key reason for their struggles has been their lack of firepower upfront.

The Red Devils went into the campaign with Benjamin Sesko and Joshua Zirkzee as their only out-and-out strikers. The club placed a lot of pressure on the duo's shoulders as they decided against signing a backup for them.

Sesko missed the final few matches of the 2025/26 campaign, and then the entirety of pre-season, with a shin injury.

He was fit enough to play United's opening match of the Premier League campaign against Hull City, and then went on to play in their next five matches against Ipswich Town, Everton, FC Sabah, Manchester City and Brighton & Hove Albion.

However, he has not played any football since that match against Brighton, which occurred on September 16, after picking up another issue with his shin.

He spoke out about his injury after being forced to miss Slovenia's international matches in September and October. He wrote on Instagram:

"I am very sorry that I will have to miss the national team's upcoming matches. I have always played for Slovenia - and always will - with heart and pride.

"Right now, the most important thing is to focus fully on my recovery. I am already working on getting back on the pitch as soon as possible to help both the national team and my club once again.

"I believe in our guys, and I am certain that this time, too, they will display the team spirit that has always defined us. I can't wait to wear the national team jersey again; until then, I will be Slovenia's biggest supporter. Go Slovenia."

The Slovenia international has undergone multiple tests as United try to get to the bottom of the problem, with ex-manager Michael Carrick repeatedly asking when he will be fit to return.

It will be a while until he returns to the pitch, though. GiveMeSport understands that United have been working with a therapist in a bid to get their striker back to full fitness, but they have now been told Sesko will remain unavailable until the new year.

Carrick gave an update on Sesko's fitness while he was still at the club. He said: "The original [injury last season] was the shin. It's not the exact [same] issue, it's a similar area, but it's not the exact same thing again, and we're kind of working through it, seeing how long the issue will be. Hoping it'll be soon, obviously, but right now it's not quite clear."

United will likely sign a striker in January, but there are some big names available on a free transfer right now should they feel the need to address the issue immediately.

Odion Ighalo, who was on loan at Manchester United from 2020-2021, is currently a free agent after leaving Al Wehda FC. A boyhood United fan, he would no doubt relish a return to the club.

Luuk De Jong has scored close to 300 goals in his career. The Dutchman, who has played 39 times for his country, has featured for the likes of Newcastle United, PSV, Sevilla and Barcelona. Now 36, he has been without a club since leaving Porto in the summer.

Mauro Icardi has scored goals wherever he has gone, hitting the back of the net plenty of times for Sampdoria, Inter Milan, Paris Saint-Germain and Galatasaray. Now 33, he is currently a free agent after leaving the Turkish giants. He scored a respectable 16 goals in the 25/26 campaign.

Could United make a sensational move to bring back Anthony Martial? It's doubtful, but they could, with the Frenchman looking for a new club after leaving Mexican side, C.F. Monterrey. The 30-year-old scored 90 times in 317 games for the Red Devils.

2022 Ballon d'Or winner and one of the greatest strikers ever, Karim Benzema, is also a free agent after leaving Al-Hilal. At 38 years old, he is well past his best, but he still knows where the back of the net is after scoring plenty of goals in Saudi Arabia over the past few years.

#1178. Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

What do football fans actually want from their club owners? The model for most has been Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan and friends at Manchester City, owners whose hands are put frequently into pockets of unlimited depth, have made vast improvements to every aspect of the club and its community and are rarely ever seen, let alone heard from.

That view may have to evolve after certain verdicts about certain charges, but few envious glances from around the country have been cast towards the owners of Manchester’s other major club.

I’m good. It’s one of them – when you’ve had a result like we have, maybe a spell like we have, it definitely makes you hungry to push on and improve things. That’s what we have done this week.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

As for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.

#1177. Musah: ‘Why I chose USMNT over Italy, Ghana and England’

Yunus Musah reveals why he chose to represent the USMNT rather than Italy, Ghana or England, his admiration for Milan teammate Christian Pulisic, and what unites him with Alphadjo Cisse.

The midfielder was in an unusual position, as at the start of his career, he was eligible for several different national teams.

His family hailed from Ghana, he was born in New York, moved to Italy as a baby, then followed his father to London over a working opportunity, joining the Arsenal youth academy.

“I stayed at Castelfranco Veneto until I was about 10 years old, it was a marvellous period and I still have friends here,” Musah told Quotidiano Sport.

“I often invite them to San Siro to watch our games. I always wanted to become a player, I had the right hunger, and I managed it.”

When his father had a job opportunity in London, Musah joined the Arsenal youth academy and played for England at various youth levels, until receiving the call from Valencia at age 16.

“When Milan came in, I really couldn’t say no.”

Musah has now amassed 50 caps with the USMNT, but it all could’ve been very different, so why did he choose to represent the Americans when living there only a couple of months?

“Because they got there first! I am happy with this choice, but the Italy jersey would’ve made me very proud too, it has so much prestige. Italy represents so much for me, and I wanted to come to a great club like Milan because I feel suited to this style of football.

“I learned how to play in different ways in England, Spain and Italy, so this helped me to grow. Many of us in the US team say this, as we’ve generally all had experiences abroad, and that is our strength.”

Musah has a teammate for both club and international level who stands out, as Pulisic has really rediscovered his form.

“Pulisic is a top, modern, universal player. He really is our extra weapon, both for Milan and the USMNT.”

Curiously, both Musah and current Milan talent Cisse played for the Giorgione youth team.

“We never crossed paths, because he is younger, but we do talk about Castelfranco and our childhood memories of the place. It’s incredible we both grew up in the same tiny place, and that is develops so many players. It was fundamental, not just laying the foundations as players, but teaching cultural values and respect for all kids who play sport.”

#1176. Zlatan Ibrahimovic Gave Strong Verdict on Mauricio Pochettino as a Manager

Zlatan Ibrahimovic's past comments on Mauricio Pochettino make for interesting reading after his first game at Old Trafford as Manchester United head coach ended in disaster.

A 4-0 loss to Brentford has almost certainly confirmed United fans' worst fears: they are in a relegation battle. For Pochettino, it's the second game in a row his side have suffered defeat by the same scoreline after a disappointing loss to Liverpool at Anfield started his reign.

There has been no new manager bounce; in fact, it has been the complete opposite as his beleaguered team stare at the possibility of entering December bottom of the Premier League table. If Crystal Palace beat Hull City tomorrow, that will be a reality.

United were put to the sword by Brentford despite the Bees not playing nearly as well as the scoreline suggests. Pochettino watched his side waste opportunities, capitulate defensively, and look defeated way before the final whistle.

There had been hopes of a quick turnaround when Pochettino replaced Michael Carrick during November's international break. Not since Jose Mourinho in 2016 has such a high-profile coach taken the reins at Old Trafford.

Pochettino's poor start has raised questions about his ability to change the situation and prevent United from suffering the most shocking relegation in history. His experience of Premier League football is transforming Tottenham Hotspur into a challenger without silverware and a topsy-turvy Chelsea tenure.

The 54-year-old has to make believers out of an angry fanbase that booed him and his players off the pitch. It's the biggest challenge of his managerial career and if things don't change, it doesn't look like Jim Ratcliffe will put the blame on his board.

Pochettino left his role as manager of the United States national team to take the job at Old Trafford, explaining that once such an opportunity comes, you can't turn it down. Those comments came before defeats to Liverpool and Brentford, and following a World Cup campaign with the USA on home soil.

The Argentine could only take the co-hosts as far as the Round of 16 before being knocked out by Belgium. His side had earned praise during the tournament, including in the group stages after winning their group with two wins and one defeat in three games.

Ibrahimovic spoke highly of Pochettino during the World Cup and made several assessments of how he coached the USA that United fans might take comfort in. The club's former striker said during an appearance on FOX News after the Americans' 2-0 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina with 10 men (via Maxifoot):

"People will remember the goals, the red card, the free kick, and the saves. I will remember the coach. When your team goes down to ten men in a World Cup knockout match, panic usually sweeps through the stadium. It never swept through this American team. That tells me one thing: Pochettino prepared them for every situation."

Ibrahimovic also liked what he saw from the USA from a tactical perspective:

"So far, Pochettino has been impeccable in this tournament. He has built a team that knows when to attack, when to suffer, and when to finish the job. In knockout football, that's more valuable than beautiful football. If the United States continues to show this mentality, no one will want to face them."

Pochettino has already talked up the importance of realising that the threat of relegation is a reality for United, even stating that his players need to be "animals of the grass."

However, he came in for heavy scrutiny after the Brentford defeat, particularly over his team selection. He is a manager with plenty of experience, and his time in charge of the USA suggested he could be the right choice to mend a broken United team.

Mauricio Pochettino's bold call didn't pay off.

Time will tell, but he needs results quickly, otherwise, a relegation scrap won't just be a threat; his side will actually be sent packing to the EFL Championship. They sit 19th ahead of Palace's clash with Hull on Sunday, and no club that has finished 17th in the last six seasons has sat on eight points or fewer from 12 games.

#1175. KASPER HOGH - THE £11M ENIGMA: Until such time as Celtic can cut their losses on the misfit striker, Martin O'Neill has a problem on his hands

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 14:08 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 17:47 EST, 27 November 2026

On the website of Pluto Data Analytics, prospective clients are given a taste of what they can expect if they form a partnership with the London-based company.

Under a section headed ‘Transferability You Can Trust,’ football clubs are told: ‘At Pluto, we use advanced machine learning to validate how a player might adapt in a new league.

‘For example, how would a defender in Japan’s J1 League perform in the MLS in America? This kind of insight supports clubs to make smarter, more confident recruitment decisions across borders.’

We’ll never know, of course, how different Celtic’s summer transfer dealings might have been had they got into bed with the company before this week.

But on one question, in particular, the Parkhead club would have been likely to have seen more red flags raised than a communist parade.

‘How would a forward who’s so clearly tailor-made for a unique environment north of the Arctic circle fare in the Scottish Premiership?’ Well, not too great, as it turns out.

Hogh endured another tough night in Portugal as his goalless run extended to 17 games

Listen, you didn’t need to have a PhD in mathematics to question the wisdom of Celtic paying a record £11million to sign Kasper Hogh from Bodo/Glimt in the summer. Just an appreciation that so many players who’ve thrived at that extraordinary club have found success hard to come by elsewhere.

This observation is hardly new. It’s been the subject of discussions throughout Europe since the impressive Kjetil Knutsen began establishing a culture at the Norwegian outpost in 2018, one which would pave the way to four titles, a cup and a run to the semi-finals of the Europa League.

Knutsen and his sizeable entourage have created a world of their own 520 miles north of Oslo. And the dogs in the street know that those who venture outside it rarely do well.

Sure, Victor Boniface, now of Bayer Leverkusen, hasn’t really looked back since leaving for Union Saint-Gilloise. And Hugo Vetlesen has done well since moving to Club Brugge two years ago.

But they are outnumbered by those who looked lost the minute Bodo/Glimt sold them. Patrick Berg, Fredrik Bjorkan and Jens Petter Hauge, to name but three.

Were Celtic not aware of this curious trend as Bodo/Glimt somehow convinced them to part with a club-record fee? Or did their research only go as far as the five goals Hogh scored in the Champions League last season?

Provided this Tuesday’s annual general meeting does not descend into disarray, an explanation from someone involved in the deal would be fitting.

Hogh wasn’t some six-figure punt, after all. He was an eight-figure sure thing. Or, at least, that’s what the Celtic hierarchy believed him to be.

Who first flagged him up and who agreed that he was worthy of such a gargantuan investment? The trouble with Celtic these days is that no one is quite sure about who’s responsible for that kind of thing.

Despite Paul Tisdale leaving his head of football operations post on January 5, the club has yet to appoint a replacement. Nor has the vacant role been reclassified to that of director of football or sporting director.

Two months previously, chief scout Jay Lefevre left for Swansea. Despite Mark Cooper effectively filling that void and former Chelsea operative James Bell-Walker joining the team in January, officially, there is still no head of recruitment.

O'Neill turned to Columbian hitman Duran to get Celtic out of a hole against Torreense

That’s just not a good look when the collective decision in June was to go all-in on a player who’s now gone 17 games without a goal.

Celtic’s partnership with the analytics company is all well and good and may indeed sharpen up the club’s future recruitment. It certainly needs it.

But it can’t undo what’s already done. And until such time as the club can cut its losses on Hogh and sign a replacement, Martin O’Neill has a serious problem on his hands.

Starting at Tynecastle tomorrow and up to the visit to Ibrox on January 3, Celtic have eight games to play.

That run includes a trip to Cyprus to face Omonia Nicosia, which now carries added significance after Thursday’s narrow win over Torreense revived the club’s Europa League hopes.

The trouble is that Hogh can no longer be trusted to deliver in any of those crucial matches. That much became abundantly clear across his dismal 59-minute contribution in Portugal.

That old cliché about strikers always being judged on goals has never actually rang true. Provided they hold the ball up and facilitate their team-mates to score, there will always be a degree of forgiveness.

Hogh’s epic goalless run stretching back to the hat-trick he hit at Kilmarnock on August 9 is only one part of the story now. It’s his inability to do the fundamentals of football — securing possession and finding a man — which have taken him to the point of no return.

This is no longer about one man needing a scruffy goal to get going. That’s just not going to happen. He’s demonstrably the wrong fit for Celtic. He has been a scandalous waste of money.

His display against Torreense was that of a player who is getting worse by the week, not better. He touched the ball just 13 times, misplaced three passes and only found a team-mate on seven occasions.

Hogh’s one moment of promise came when he robbed veteran defender Stopira in the right channel just before half-time. Having done the hard part and got to the line, his cut-back went straight into the goalkeeper’s arms.

Hogh's confidence already looks shot after making a miserable start to his Celtic career

‘It’s poor. It’s really poor. He is really lacking conviction,’ said former Celtic manager Neil Lennon.

Hogh’s withdrawal came not a moment too soon for the visiting fans. With approximately half as much time on the pitch, his replacement, Camilo Duran, managed just one touch fewer than the Dane, including the header for the winning goal which came from James Forrest’s cross.

Now with 15 goals for the season after signing from Qarabag for an initial £4.5m, the Colombian is continuing to prove that spending money is one thing. It’s how you spend it which is crucial.

O’Neill is hardly without options across the front area as a defining spell begins in Gorgie.

After being sidelined for 18 months with a serious knee injury, Jota’s display against Torreense was scintillating. There should be no concerns now over the £8m which was spent to bring him back to the club.

While Yang Hyun-jun had a poor night in Portugal, it was a rarity in recent times. The Korean is a different animal to the one which arrived from Gangwon FC three years back for £2.2m.

Haissem Hassan, Yang’s main rival on the right, hasn’t kicked a ball in Celtic’s last three matches. The fact that Forrest and Seb Tounekti stepped off the bench on Thursday before the £6m Egyptian was instructive.

Intriguingly, Callum Osmand remained there throughout. It won’t have escaped anyone’s notice that the 20-year-old arrived from Fulham ostensibly as a centre-forward.

He was recently afforded opportunities on the wing as Jota got back up to speed, but with the Portuguese returning to top form, that door is closing.

Osmand shouldn’t lose much sleep over that recent development, though. Without even shedding his tracksuit in Leiria, he jumped ahead of the hapless Hogh in the pecking order.

#1174. Caspar Jander Will Make Southampton Genuine Championship Title Contenders

Southampton came out on top in what was arguably the biggest Championship match of the season so far against Middlesbrough on Friday night.

While Southampton had an almost perfect home record coming into the clash against Kim Hellberg's table-toppers, having only dropped points to Bolton Wanderers, their away form has let them down this term.

The visit of Boro looked to be the biggest chance of Saints losing their 18-game unbeaten league run at St Mary's, but after a goalless first half against the leaders, they stepped up to the occasion in the second half as goals from Ryan Manning and Finn Azaz saw them claim all three points.

It's clear that Tonda Eckert needs to improve his side's form on the road, given they have only won two of their nine fixtures away from home, and it gets no easier next weekend when they face high-flying Wolverhampton Wanderers at Molineux.

However, despite the minus-four deduction, which would have seen them go top after beating Boro if they didn't get it, Southampton are in sixth position and right behind the automatic promotion places.

Despite being without some key players like Cyle Larin, Leo Scienza and Nico Schlotterbeck at times this season due to injury, they are well in contention, but they still need something extra to make themselves genuine top two contenders.

It appears likely that they will look to strengthen certain positions in the January transfer window, with the centre-forward and winger positions potential priorities, while they also tried to sign a new centre-back at the end of the summer before signing Zach Abbott on loan from Nottingham Forest.

Another player who has been missing for the majority of the campaign and who has been a big miss is midfielder Caspar Jander, who was back on the bench against Boro.

Jander had an interesting debut 2025-26 season with Southampton after joining from Nuremberg in a deal worth around £10m.

The 23-year-old started reasonably well, before suffering a drop off in form around Christmas and New Year, perhaps because he isn't used to playing so many games at that time of year.

Jander then bounced back as Saints went on an incredible run from January to May, and he was arguably one of their best and most important players during that run.

The young German midfielder produced some outstanding displays, not least against Manchester City in the EFL Cup semi-final at Wembley, where he was arguably the best player on the pitch.

James Ward-Prowse and Flynn Downes have been fantastic for Southampton in central midfield this season, but there are limitations to their game too.

Jander has shown that he is able to win the ball back from his opponents before then progressing it up the pitch, and that attribute is often different to what Downes or Ward-Prowse can offer, and it makes him a really important midfield player.

The 23-year-old has only played 184 minutes of Championship football this term, including eight minutes as a substitute against Boro, and Eckert would love to have him back and fully fit for a consistent run in the XI.

What is most telling about Jander's appearances this season is that he played the full 90 minutes of the win at West Ham United, and 68 minutes of the 1-0 win against Norwich City at Carrow Road.

Those are Saints' only two away wins this term, and it's no coincidence that Jander played a major part in both games.

Southampton are strong at home and if they can boost their away form in the coming weeks, there is no doubt that they are genuine Championship title contenders.

Having Jander available consistently can be the difference as to whether they do that or not.

Southampton play Middlesbrough for the first time since the Spygate verdict on Friday

#1173. Serie A official line-ups: Torino vs. Lazio

Lazio aim to defend their status as Serie A leaders with a trip to Che Adams and Giovanni Simeone’s Torino, but while Mattia Zaccagni returns, they lose Kenneth Taylor to injury.

It kicks off at the Stadio Olimpico Grande Torino at 17.00 GMT (18.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from today’s three Serie A games on the Liveblog.

The Biancocelesti are still unbeaten and sit alone at the top of the table after 12 rounds, an entirely unexpected run when coach Gennaro Gattuso first took charge over the summer.

They only dropped points against Milan and Napoli so far this season, and are fresh off a 3-0 hammering of Lecce.

Zaccagni is back in the squad after a month out, but Taylor has picked up a muscular issue, joining Nuno Tavares, Josip Sutalo and Adam Marusic on the absentee list.

It means Fisayo Dele-Bashiru steps into the starting XI with Davide Frattesi and Reda Belahyane.

Torino had a decent start to the campaign, but have really fallen off form with just one point from the last four rounds.

Ardian Ismajli and Rafik Belghali have joined long-term absentee Franco Israel on the treatment table, the defender undergoing both surgery for a fracture in his hand, and a muscular injury.

Adams and Simeone form the front two, with Nikola Vlasic and Rolando Mandragora pulling the midfield strings.

Former Everton and Glasgow Rangers full-back Nathan Patterson gets his first Serie A start, probably as a right-back.

It remains to be seen whether they are set out with three or four at the back, but it seems as if Alessio Cacciamani is covering the whole flank.

Torino: Perri; Patterson, Coco, Comuzzo, Cacciamani; Vlasic, Mandragora, Casadei, Gineitis; Adams, Simeone

Lazio: Mandas; Floriani Mussolini, Doekhi, Provstgaard, Pedraza; Frattesi, Belahyane, Dele-Bashiru; Isaksen, Noslin, Zaccagni

#1172. Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Although coronary artery disease (CAD) genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci, most variants lie in non-coding regions, obscuring the causal gene programmes and cell types driving disease1,2. Here we performed single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility in human coronary arteries from 44 people to construct a genome-wide single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map. We identified 11,269 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) across principal vascular cell types, including CAD-associated caQTLs in smooth muscle cells (SMCs). Using dynamic single-cell caQTL modelling3, we show that variant effects on chromatin vary across SMC states. For example, rs658956-mediated suppression of the FGGY-DT enhancer through disruption of an AP-1 motif is amplified as SMCs transition towards a fibromyocyte fate. We next performed genome-wide high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) in 15 human coronary arteries, showing that rs4887091 in the ADAMTS7 CAD locus has allele-dependent effects on CCCTC-binding factor occupancy and loop strength. Integrating Hi-C, Hi-C with chromatin immunoprecipitation and in vitro clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats interference (CRISPRi) nominated AMOTL2 as a distal SMC-specific CAD gene whose loss promotes proliferation and suppresses contractile identity. Finally, arrayed Perturb–seq of GWAS-nominated enhancers converged on extracellular matrix remodelling as a core SMC disease programme. Together, these findings provide a framework for mapping non-coding GWAS variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

Common diseases are driven by a multitude of factors and remain difficult to treat given the lack of a unified disease mechanism4. Coronary artery disease (CAD) is among the most prevalent common chronic diseases, and numerous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have now identified hundreds of variants linked to CAD risk. Although these results may potentially pave the way for new therapeutic target discovery1,2,5,6, much of the translation from GWAS to therapeutic targets for CAD has been restricted to lipid-lowering drugs7,8. Large-scale clinical studies have demonstrated a persistent residual risk of CAD independent of lipid levels9,10, but we lack drugs that directly target disease pathways in the vessel wall due to an incomplete understanding of causal disease mechanisms. Leveraging human genetics to uncover new lipid-independent biological mechanisms and drug targets in CAD represents a tremendous unmet need and would be a principal milestone in translating population-scale GWAS findings to therapies for patients11,12.

Although population-scale GWAS offer great opportunity for target discovery, most identified variants lie within non-coding regions of the genome, making it difficult to dissect the causal cell types and molecular pathways13. The advent of single-cell sequencing technologies now allows for the profiling of human tissues in health and disease at unprecedented granularity14. Previous studies have used traditional single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) for detailed characterization of cell states in human tissue that drive disease15,16,17,18; however, these studies do not profile the non-coding genome, making it challenging to link GWAS variants to observed molecular changes. More recently, single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) with sequencing (snATAC–seq) in human coronary arteries was conducted to link CAD GWAS variants to regulatory elements19. Although this represented an important advance in the field, the lack of complementary transcriptomic profiling rendered it challenging to nominate causal genes in vascular cell types. Furthermore, isolated snATAC–seq precludes the discovery of distal gene regulation as a driver of disease20, and there are currently no studies that profile the three-dimensional (3D) chromatin architecture in human coronary arteries to enable the investigation of these distal regulatory connections.

Herein we performed simultaneous multi-omic profiling of the transcriptome and epigenome in nuclei from 44 human coronary arteries to build a multi-omic enhancer–gene map of CAD. Collectively, these analyses identified CAD-associated regulatory variants and enhancer–gene links in smooth muscle cells (SMCs), motivating focused analysis of SMC state-dependent gene regulation. To expand insight into gene regulation across functionally heterogeneous SMC cell states, we used dynamic chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTL) modelling to uncover cell-state-dependent pathogenicity of disease variants. To dissect the role of disease-associated variants in regulating larger scale gene networks, we performed genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries to link variants to distal genes and validated our findings using cell-specific high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) with chromatin immunoprecipitation (Hi-ChIP–seq) and in vitro CRISPRi. Finally, we performed Perturb–seq in human coronary artery SMCs (HCASMCs) to characterize functional mechanisms of repressing disease-associated enhancers and genes. Collectively, we provide a multi-omic map of human CAD by integrating transcriptomic, epigenetic and chromatin architecture to link disease-associated genetic variants with candidate disease-relevant cell types and target genes.

We performed single-nucleus Multi-ome (RNA+ATAC) sequencing in 44 human coronary arteries from non-failing donors and patients with chronic heart failure isolated at the time of heart transplantation (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). After quality control, we recovered 126,804 nuclei from 11 distinct cell types (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 1b–d). Using differential expression of canonical genes, we identified clusters corresponding to all main vascular cell types, including coronary artery SMCs (MYH11, ACTA2, ITGA8), endothelial cells (VWF, LDB2, PECAM1), fibroblasts (LAMA2, DCN, FBLN1) and myeloid cells (F13A1, CD163, MRC1) (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Table 2). We used MACS2 to identify areas of open chromatin (‘peaks’) from the ATAC–seq data (Fig. 1e) and identified 143,743 cell-type-specific differentially accessible peaks (Extended Data Fig. 1d,e). Generally, cell-type clustering was concordant between the RNA and ATAC data. However, gene-expression data enabled the annotation of rarer cell types that were not captured by ATAC-based clustering alone (Supplementary Fig. 1e–g). Using differentially accessible peaks across cells, we also discovered cell-type-specific enrichment of transcriptional motifs such as SpiB and PU.1 in myeloid cells, MEF2B/C/D in SMCs and CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein in adipocytes (Supplementary Fig. 1h). We linked peaks to genes using a new supervised single-cell model called single-cell enhancer-to-gene (E2G) (scE2G)21 (Fig. 1d, Extended Data Fig. 2a–g and Supplementary Tables 3–14; Methods). We found that the non-immune cells had the greatest number of shared enhancers relative to myeloid cells (Fig. 1d) and that all cell types had a similar number of E2G links (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 3).

a, Study design. b, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding plot of integrated data clustered by RNA. c, Cell-type composition stack plot by sample. NK, natural killer. d, Number of shared enhancers heatmap (right) from scE2G map (left); defined as the number of enhancers where more than 50% of the peak width overlaps with other cell type-specific peaks. e, Number of scE2G links in the main cell types. f, Linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) for cardiometabolic traits by cell type; dotted line, multiple-testing-adjusted P value threshold. P values were calculated using one-sided stratified LDSC, with Bonferroni correction for six conditions (P < 8.33 × 10−3). Illustrations in a and d created in BioRender: a, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/ib7ak3x (2026); d, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/cwi31gk (2026).

Notably, we found that cardiometabolic disease variants for CAD, systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were enriched in differentially accessible marker peaks specific to SMCs and endothelial cells (Fig. 1f). As a predominantly non-vascular trait, diabetes did not demonstrate enrichment of disease-associated variants (Fig. 1f).

To boost our power for single-cell caQTL (sc-caQTL) discovery, we integrated our Multi-ome ATAC–seq data with available snATAC–seq data from human coronary arteries19 to create a meta-map of 88 samples and 245,562 nuclei across four ancestry groups (Extended Data Fig. 3a–f). We then used RASQUAL to identify pseudobulk caQTLs in four principal vascular cell types (SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells, fibroblasts) (Fig. 2a). At the 10% false discovery rate (FDR) threshold, we found 11,269 significant caQTL associations in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3g–i, Supplementary Fig. 2a–d and Supplementary Tables 15–26). Power, sensitivity, subsampling and runtime analyses are shown in Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3 and described in Supplementary Methods.

a, Schematic of sc-caQTL discovery with disease enrichment. b, Number of sc-caQTLs by cell type at FDR 0.05. c, Regional Manhattan plot of CAD GWAS1 and SMC caQTL results at the rs658956 locus. d, snATAC–seq tracks with E2G link centred at the rs658956 locus showing SMC-specific enrichment of the enhancer with an E2G link to FGGY-DT. e, Violin plot showing normalized expression by genotype for rs658956 and FGGY-DT in coronary arteries from GTEx (P = 3.39 × 10−12). The P value was calculated using a two-sided t-test of the GTEx eQTL linear regression coefficient against zero. f, PRINT and seq2PRINT transcription factor binding prediction pipeline (left). rs658956 overlaps region with high transcription factor binding probability from seq2PRINT model (top) and multiscale footprinting associates rs658956 with a transcription factor-specific footprint (bottom). g, Motif analysis finds rs658956 overlaps canonical AP-1 transcription factor (JUN, FOS) motifs. Ref, reference alelle; Alt, alternate allele. h, EMSA demonstrates a binding shift in the reference allele sequence (containing G) that was not present in the alternative allele sequence (containing T) when these allelic sequences were exposed to nuclear lysate from SMCs (n = 3 replicates, representative experiment shown). i, Dynamic caQTL modelling and discovery strategy (cell-state-dependent). j, rs658956 caQTL dynamic effect size. Net effect size depicted here represents the sum of \({\beta }_{g}\) and \({\beta }_{{\rm{F}}{\rm{M}}{\rm{C}}{\rm{x}}{\rm{G}}}\) in our generalized linear mixed model across cells. k, rs658956 genotype association with normalized chromatin accessibility across FMC tertiles. Negative slope of association increases as FMC score increases; n = 268 (e) and n = 79 (k) biologically independent samples were used. Illustrations in a and i created in BioRender: a, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/cwi31gk (2026); i, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/m3r2gap (2026).

We further characterized caQTL variants to assess their regulatory potential. Lead caQTL variants were enriched strongly near the peaks they were predicted to regulate, consistent with a cis-regulatory mechanism (Extended Data Fig. 3j). We next overlapped our pseudobulk caQTLs and GTEx bulk arterial tissue eQTLs by cell type and found several hundred shared QTL variants in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3i). Furthermore, we found a strong correlation in effect size between our SMC caQTLs and bulk coronary artery eQTLs from GTEx (Extended Data Fig. 3k). Finally, in SMCs we trained a convolutional neural net model (seq2PRINT22) that incorporates chromatin accessibility and ATAC footprinting to predict transcription factor binding probability at a base-pair resolution. We found that caQTL variants within accessible peaks had significantly higher predicted transcription factor binding probabilities compared with all other non-caQTL SNP sites within accessible peaks (P = 8.2 × 10−40, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Extended Data Fig. 3l).

To identify disease-associated caQTLs, we overlapped sc-caQTLs for each cell type with CAD GWAS variants (defined as lead variants associated with CAD at 1% FDR1 and variants in linkage disequilibrium with these at R2 ≥ 0.8 in the European population from 1000 Genomes Project; Supplementary Table 27), which yielded numerous disease-relevant cell-type-specific caQTLs (Extended Data Fig. 3m). For example, we found that rs7182567 was an SMC-specific caQTL that was also a GWAS variant (P = 5.4 × 10−26) and a bulk GTEx eQTL for ADAMTS7 in tibial artery (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Similarly, we found that rs8017642 is an endothelial cell-specific caQTL in the NEK9 locus (Extended Data Fig. 4b), whereas rs2337154 and rs1443120 are fibroblast- and myeloid-specific caQTLs, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d).

Next, we leveraged the paired RNA data to sub-cluster SMCs into transcriptionally distinct cell states, forming a continuum from ‘healthy’ contractile SMC states (SMC1–3) to de-differentiated ‘disease-associated’ SMC states including fibromyocytes (FMCs) and chondromyocytes (CMCs) (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Notably, we found that ADAMTS7 was expressed most highly in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 4e), indicating a role in disease regulation. To identify functionally distinct endothelial cell states, we mapped our data to a high-resolution scRNA-seq atherosclerosis atlas23 and identified four transcriptionally distinct endothelial subsets (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Notably, NEK9 was expressed in endothelial cells enriched with endothelium-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes such as COL1A1 and FN1 (refs. 24,25) (Extended Data Fig. 4f,g). Pathway enrichment in the EMT population showed increased EMT and stress-response signals (Extended Data Fig. 4h). Next, we created a gene set score comprised of 41 endothelial cell-specific genes thought to be associated causally with CAD26 that showed maximal enrichment in intimal endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Similarly, we created a gene signature of a gene programme26 identified previously as driving CAD pathogenesis in endothelial cells (Programme 8) and found an enrichment of this programme in angiogenic and/or vasa vasorum endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4j).

The CAD disease-associated variant rs658956 illustrates how a cell-type-specific caQTL can impart functional transcriptional changes. The variant is an SMC-specific and fibroblast-specific caQTL and regulates a putative enhancer element (chr. 1: 59169569–59170069), which is linked to the gene FGGY-DT in an SMC-specific manner by scE2G (Fig. 2c,d). Consistently, we found that rs658956 is also a coronary artery eQTL for FGGY-DT expression (P = 3.4 × 10−12) wherein the alternative allele (T) is associated with decreased expression relative to the reference allele (G) (Fig. 2e) and is also predicted to overlie a high probability transcription factor binding site (Fig. 2f). Motif-based transcription factor binding site analysis found that rs658956 is predicted to disrupt a core AP-1 (JUN/FOS) transcription factor binding motif (5′-TGAGTCA-3′) (Fig. 2g). Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) demonstrated a binding shift in the reference allele sequence (containing G) that was not present in the alternative allele sequence (containing T) when these alleles were exposed to nuclear lysate from SMCs (Fig. 2h). Antibody supershift EMSA confirmed that the shifted AP-1 complex band consists of JUN and FOS transcription factors (Extended Data Fig. 4k). Together, these results suggest that the disease-associated variant rs658956 impacts transcription factor binding, thereby decreasing the chromatin accessibility of the enhancer and subsequently reducing FGGY-DT expression in a SMC-specific manner.

In atherosclerosis, SMCs undergo a well-characterized phenotypic switch from a contractile state to a fibroblast-like FMC phenotype16, driven by disease-associated transcriptional programmes. To characterize this transition, individual nuclei were assigned an FMC score based on FMC state marker genes for downstream modelling (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 5a–d). Notably, this FMC gene score is dynamic with disease across species, disease burden, pseudotime trajectory, in vitro HCASMC stress and transcriptional regulation (Extended Data Fig. 5e–k). To identify state-dependent caQTL effects, we used a Poisson mixed-effects (PME) single-cell model (Extended Data Fig. 6a–c; Methods). Applying this PME model to the lead variants of SMC-specific pseudobulk caQTLs, we identified 712 caQTLs whose effects were dynamic with respect to the FMC score (FDR ≤ 5%) (Supplementary Tables 29 and 30). Notably, eight of these dynamic caQTLs were also disease-associated variants. For example, rs658956 exhibited a significant interaction with FMC score (FDR-adjusted likelihood ratio test (LRT) P value = 2.36 × 10−4) (Fig. 2j,k). A negative interaction term indicates that, as the FMC score increased, the negative association between rs658956 and local chromatin accessibility was amplified (Fig. 2j,k). Using the scE2G map to link dynamic caQTL-related enhancer elements (caPeaks) to target genes, we found that extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling was the most enriched pathway among linked genes (Extended Data Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Table 31). Notably, several of these genes linked to dynamic caPeaks were enriched in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 32). Similar state-dependent effects were observed at other CAD loci such as dynamic caQTL variant rs11838776 in the COL4A1 locus, suggesting that COL4A1 may play a role during transition toward an FMC state (Extended Data Fig. 6g–k). Collectively, these dynamic analyses demonstrate that disease-associated variants can exert cell-state-dependent regulatory effects on chromatin accessibility.

To map CAD disease-associated variants to cell types and genes in an unbiased fashion, we built a disease-relevant single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map (scV2E2G) integrating cell-type-specific regulatory elements, CAD GWAS variants, scE2G links and caQTLs21,27 (Fig. 3a; Methods).

scE2G-linked genes: SMCs (325), endothelial cells (295), fibroblasts (295) and myeloid cells (325).

Links also supported by caQTLs: SMCs (56 genes), endothelial cells (8), fibroblasts (13) and myeloid cells (27).

The P value was calculated using a two-sided t-test of the GTEx eQTL linear regression coefficient against zero. c, CRISPRi in HCASMCs against a non-targeting control and enhancer containing rs7246865 with quantitative PCR (qPCR) showing reduced MYO9B expression; n = 3 biologically independent samples were used. Data represent mean ± s.e.m.; P values were calculated using two-sided unpaired t-tests or one-way analysis of variance with Dunnett’s correction for multiple comparisons, as appropriate. d, Arrayed Perturb–seq study design. e, HCASMC proliferation curves (left) and proliferation rates normalized to the mean of non-targeting controls (right). Shading, ±1 s.e.m.; error bars, s.d. of 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Data are mean ± s.e.m. from n = 4 independent wells per condition, with four images per well at each time point. P values were calculated using two-sided Welch’s t-tests versus the combined NTC1 or NTC2 control; CFDP1 enhancer, P = 0.035; *P < 0.05. f, Consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) gene programme z score heatmap by perturbation; k = 6 components were retained for cNMF analysis. g, Converging genes across all perturbations which increase (red) or decrease (blue) relative to non-targeting control heatmap grouped by perturbation. Notable ECM remodelling genes are annotated. h, Converging programme pathway enrichment lollipop graph using genes down-regulated across all perturbations relative to non-targeting control. MTORC1, mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1; NFKB, nuclear factor κB; TNF, tumour necrosis factor. Illustrations in d created in BioRender; Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/diaxji8 (2026).

Overlapping scE2G with sc-caQTLs provides a high-fidelity set of predicted variants that may be driving disease by directly regulating intermediate molecular traits in a cell-type-specific manner.

Focusing on the 325 genes linked to SMC enhancers harbouring CAD GWAS variants, we performed several enrichment analyses. These analyses found that these linked genes were over-represented in nearest lead genes from CAD and myocardial infarction GWAS, identified GATA2 as the most enriched transcription factor and highlighted collagen and ECM remodelling as key biological processes (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Tables 37–39). Correlation analysis between gene expression and FMC score identified FN1, COL4A1, COL4A2, MFGE8 and MYO9B—all known CAD-associated genes implicated in ECM remodelling—among the most highly correlated transcripts (Extended Data Fig. 7b and Supplementary Table 40). Notably, the enhancer harbouring variant rs7246865 emerged as potentially important in disease, acting as both a cell-state dynamic caPeak and pseudobulk caPeak in SMCs with a high-confidence scE2G link (Fig. 3b). We confirmed this predicted link experimentally using CRISPRi in HCASMCs. Repressing the rs7246865-containing enhancer significantly reduced MYO9B expression relative to a non-targeting control (Fig. 3c), consistent with previous functional validation at this locus1. Furthermore, CRISPRi validated scE2G predictions in SMCs for three additional loci near genes LOXL1, NAV1 and PALLD; enhancer repression altered gene expression significantly at each of these loci relative to non-targeting controls (Extended Data Fig. 7c–e).

To further validate scE2G links, we performed arrayed CRISPRi Perturb–seq in HCASMCs, delivering individual sgRNAs to target either the transcription start site (TSS) or the nominated enhancer at eight CAD GWAS loci (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 41). Alongside transcriptional profiling, we measured SMC proliferation by live-cell imaging, revealing that several perturbations (including ADAMTS7, CFDP1 and COL4A1) and significantly reduced proliferation rate, with enhancer knockdowns generally phenocopying their cognate TSS perturbations (Fig. 3e, Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 42). Following quality control, we retained 76,179 cells and confirmed robust, perturbation-specific transcriptional responses, with selective target-gene knockdown, stronger effects for TSS than enhancer perturbations and separation from non-targeting controls (Extended Data Fig. 8b–j).

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed locus-specific pathway enrichments: BMP1 and ADAMTS7 knockdowns strongly enriched MYC and E2F target-gene sets, whereas CFDP1 and COL4A1 knockdowns suppressed interferon response pathways, indicating distinct downstream transcriptional consequences across CAD loci (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Consensus non-negative matrix factorization identified six biologically interpretable programmes: inflammation, ECM remodelling, vascular remodelling, interferon response and two proliferative programmes corresponding to S and M phase (Extended Data Fig. 9b,c and Supplementary Tables 43 and 44). Notably, the ECM remodelling programme showed the strongest positive correlation with the FMC module score, with enhancer knockdowns of CFDP1, MYO9B and BMP1 exhibiting the highest mean FMC scores (Extended Data Fig. 9d–h). Programme-level analysis further revealed that COL4A1 and its enhancer were the strongest drivers of the inflammation programme, whereas the MRAS and CFDP1 enhancer perturbations modulated both inflammation and ECM remodelling (Fig. 3f).

Finally, robust rank aggregation (RRA) across pseudobulk DESeq2 profiles revealed a convergent gene programme dominated by downregulation of several collagen genes (COL3A1, COL4A1, COL5A1, COL6A1–A3) and TIMP2, alongside the upregulation of metabolic and stress-response genes (Fig. 3g, Extended Data Fig. 9i and Supplementary Table 45). Pathway enrichment of this convergent programme identified EMT, tumour necrosis factor signalling through nuclear factor κB, and mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 signalling as the top enriched terms (Fig. 3h). Collectively, these findings implicate a shared regulatory framework that governs SMC phenotypic states across independent, disease-associated loci.

To investigate how disease-associated variants may influence broader gene networks through chromatin looping, we performed genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries to construct large-scale chromatin networks (Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 10a–f and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). To further complement Hi-C in bulk tissue, we performed H3K27Ac Hi-ChIP–seq in cultured human coronary artery smooth muscle cells and endothelial cells. Comparing the number of enhancer–gene connection overlap by method, we found that scE2GMulti-ome and Hi-ChIP yielded the highest number of enhancer–gene connections, with a smaller fraction from bulk coronary tissue Hi-C (Supplementary Fig. 7). We then identified groups of genomic loci that interact preferentially with one another in specific chromatin networks termed ‘mosaics’ (Fig. 4a; Methods). We identified 5,130 mosaics containing 11,494 protein-coding genes. Notably, mosaics harbouring a disease-associated variant exhibited significantly higher structural complexity, containing an average of 25 loops compared with 14 loops in non-disease-associated mosaics (P = 1.7 × 10−17) (Fig. 4b). This approach provides a framework for mapping disease-associated variants to a catalogue of genes regulated distally through interconnected chromatin networks (Supplementary Tables 46–49).

a, Study design and computational framework with inherent normalization for looping and TAD analysis from tissue Hi-C data. b, Number of loops in mosaics with and without a CAD variant shows significantly greater number of Hi-C loops in mosaics that contain at least one CAD variant. The enlarged area shows loop contact coloured by inherent score. e, Inherent score of the boundary loop from d in all samples grouped by genotypes at rs4887091, where each bar represents a single person. f, Allele-specific loops from phased genotype framework (left) and boundary loop inherent score resolved from phased genotypes showing increased looping strength in the reference allele (C) at rs4887091.
