Zion Suzuki had big gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

ASTON VILLA XI TO FACE FULHAM: Suzuki, Cash, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen, Kamara, Goretzka, Alysson, Manzambi, McGinn, Jackson

Subs: Bizot, Harwood-Bellis, Mings, Barkley, Buendia, Garnacho, Mbaye, Joao Gomes, Madjo

FULHAM XI TO FACE ASTON VILLA: Leno, Castagne, Affengruber, Bassey, Robinson, Berge, Charles, Bobb, King, Iwobi, Garcia

Subs: Lecomte, Tete, Andersen, Palacios, Rodrigo Muniz, Cairney, Kevin, Larsson, Angel

Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”

Emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

But the Spaniard said: “For different reasons, not only rest.”

Whatever he meant is unclear, but both start for Villa tonight.

Fulham have won their last two league games – against Hull and Coventry.

Manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, has made one change with Sander Berge replacing Hugo Larsson in midfield.

Villa are aiming to win three successive league games for the first time in this calendar year. The omens are good as they’ve beaten Fulham in their last seven league meetings at Villa Park.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

#1144. Cucho Hernández heads both goals as Betis win 2-0 at Slovan Bratislava to go fourth

Two headers from Cucho Hernández gave Real Betis victory over Slovan Bratislava in the Champions League. The result strengthens Manuel Pellegrini's side's position in the league phase with three rounds left.

For Hernández, Tuesday night was his first start after more than a month out injured, and he marked it with a double in Bratislava. The win came in the fifth round of the Champions League league stage.

Ángel Ortiz supplied the cross for the opener, delivering it from the right for Hernández to meet at the back post. Isco then supplied the assist for his second after the break. That goal was his third of Betis’s Champions League campaign.

Hernández went off after 63 minutes, and Troy Parrott took his place. Marc Roca replaced Facundo Bernal, who had been booked in the seventh minute. Álvaro Fidalgo came on for Isco.

Pellegrini made six changes from the side that drew 1-1 with Sevilla in the derby. Isco, Abde and Antony kept their places.

The visitors dominated the game in every department. Betis completed 605 of their 670 passes, an accuracy of 90%. Slovan managed 309 passes in total. Betis put six shots on target, while Slovan managed two. The expected goals figure was 1.52 for Betis and 0.43 for the hosts.

Slovan goalkeeper Dominik Takáč made four saves. At the other end, Álvaro Vallés made a sharp save to stop Andraž Šporar, a moment UEFA’s match summary named as one of the key moments of the game. French referee Jérôme Brisard showed one yellow card to each side.

The game also brought Slovan coach Yaya Touré up against Pellegrini, his old manager at Manchester City. Touré’s side stay bottom of the table after five defeats. They have conceded 19 goals and scored only one.

Betis now have four wins and one defeat from five matches. They are well placed to fight for a top-eight finish over the last three rounds, according to AFP. A place in the top eight would send them straight into the last 16 without a play-off.

The remaining fixtures are demanding. Betis host Como on 9 December 2026 and Arsenal on 20 January 2027. They finish the league phase away to Bayern Munich on 27 January 2027.

¡¡FINAL EN BRATISLAVA!! ¡¡LA VICTORIA ES NUESTRA, EQUIPO! 🇸🇰🔝

¡Vamos, BETIS! 💚#DíaDeBetis #EuroBetis pic.twitter.com/So3QTJbA0L

— Real Betis Balompié 🌴💚 (@RealBetis) November 24, 2026

The result also continues a solid run in all competitions. Before the derby draw, Betis had beaten Elche 2-0 and Navalcarnero 3-2.

Attention now turns to LaLiga. Betis host Rayo Vallecano on Saturday 28 November.

#1143. Villarreal take record away losing run to Prague, where Slavia are 23 games without a win

Villarreal visit Slavia Prague after seven straight Champions League away defeats, a record for a Spanish club. Their hosts have gone 23 games without a win in the competition, so one of the two runs must end today.

Villarreal face Slavia Prague in the Champions League today carrying a losing run that UEFA says is a record for a Spanish club. They have lost each of their last seven away games in the competition. Their hosts carry a burden of their own. Slavia have eight draws and 15 defeats in their last 23 Champions League games. That run equals the competition’s worst, set by Steaua București between 2006 and 2013.

One of the two sequences has to end. A Slavia win would end their drought. Any other result would stop Villarreal’s run of away defeats. Kick-off is at 17:45 GMT.

That single win was a 3-1 home victory over Napoli on 13 October. The rest of the league phase has gone badly. Villarreal lost 3-2 at Borussia Dortmund on 8 September and 4-3 at Liverpool on 20 October. PSG then won 6-0 at La Cerámica on 3 November.

That leaves Villarreal 29th with three points. Another defeat would leave them close to elimination with three games to play.

The defence is the clearest problem. Villarreal have not kept a clean sheet in any of those 15 games, a club record. None of their last 35 games in the Champions League proper has ended goalless.

Falling behind early has also been fatal. Villarreal have never won a Champions League game when trailing at half-time, with two draws and 13 defeats. On eight occasions they have gone into the interval losing on the road, and every one of those matches ended in defeat.

Nathan Saliba, Juan Foyth and Ilias Akhomach are all missing in Prague, EFE reported. Gerard Moreno trained before the game and could return.

Trpišovský has six draws and 12 defeats from his 19 Champions League matches, all in charge of Slavia. UEFA describes that as the longest winless run of any coach in the competition. Slavia have also never beaten a Spanish club from the group or league phase onwards, with two draws and four defeats. The two clubs have not met since their two games in 2017.

Villarreal coach Iñigo Pérez still expects a hard night. Speaking in Prague, he said no team in the Champions League is as aggressive as Slavia. He called the game “transcendental” for how the league phase plays out. He added that the city’s cold weather would not be an excuse.

Defender Sergi Cardona said the team must learn last season’s lesson. He expects the game to be extremely demanding.

Další domácí zápas Ligy mistrů se blíží. Ve středu 25. listopadu se v Edenu střetneme s Villarrealem. Time for Revenge!

Vstupenky jsou ve volném prodeji pro všechny ověřené uživatele ve slávistické aplikaci. Zajistěte si své místo! 📲 pic.twitter.com/NwiarDjKK1

— SK Slavia Praha (@slaviaofficial) November 18, 2026

Slovenian Rade Obrenovič will referee, with his compatriot Matej Jug as video assistant referee.

Prague is the first of three away games in a row for Villarreal across LaLiga, Europe and the Copa del Rey. They do not play at La Cerámica again until 5 December. Their next league-phase game is at home to Sabah on 8 December, before a trip to Fenerbahçe on 20 January and a home game against Manchester United on 27 January.

#1142. ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

Mathematics Álvaro Lozano-Robledo thought the Riemann hypothesis was out of AI’s reach for now.Credit: Bri Diaz/UConn Photo

The news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking. For months, reports have mounted of artificial-intelligence models toppling some of the toughest problems in mathematics, plunging the field into turmoil. But the latest claim was the most shocking yet: an AI model had helped to solve the field’s most famous open problem, the Riemann hypothesis.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The proof was released on 20 November by mathematician Levent Alpöge at AI giant Anthropic in San Francisco, California, who used an advanced version of the firm’s Claude model. It came in the form of 17 million lines of code in the open-source programming language Lean, which translates mathematical arguments into computer-certifiable code. In a matter of hours, a separate set of mathematicians rushed out a human-written proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which is in the branch of number theory and pertains to the randomness of prime numbers.

Alpöge’s proof has been independently verified by the non-profit organization behind Lean and the Mathlib Initiative, which runs the reference library of formalized mathematics results written in Lean. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him,” the community said in a statement on 21 November.

The mathematics community has broadly accepted the claim, although responses differ wildly. Some celebrate Alpöge’s achievement, but others see the development as proof that humans are fighting against machines for the future of mathematics.

Nature hears reactions from five mathematicians on what solving the Riemann hypothesis means to them.

Mathematician Tasmin Chu is part of the Association for Human Mathematics, whose members commit to doing AI-free research.Credit: Elizabeth Xiao

Tasmin Chu, PhD student in mathematics at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena.

A technology that can autonomously prove the Riemann hypothesis is no trivial matter. I think that it is imperative our society acts to pause AI development as soon as possible. Over the past year, mathematical institutions have faced the impossible task of adapting to the rapidly changing capabilities of AI in real time.

It’s enormously disruptive for early-career researchers — the people who are the intellectual future of our field. Soon other sectors of society will face the same issues.

My reaction is grave concern. AI companies urgently require democratic oversight. I do not think AI’s encroachment into math is inevitable, nor is the death of human mathematical practice inevitable. It’s a choice to disempower ourselves, just as it’s a choice to continue building these technologies despite grave safety concerns. I continue to practice mathematics without LLMs, because I believe it’s critical that scientific inquiry continues in the hands of human beings. Some of us at the Association for Human Mathematics — whose organizing committee I am on — are collectively making the same decision.

Harini Desiraju, lecturer in mathematics at the University of Warwick, UK.

Given the events of the past few months, this news wasn't entirely a surprise, but we need to wait to understand the Lean proof and let the experts verify it. It is several million lines of code, after all.

I am not a number theorist, so I might not have the same emotional attachment to the Riemann hypothesis. Nevertheless, I have deep appreciation for the ubiquity and the importance of the problem in several areas of maths and physics.

As for the recent events, I want to distinguish between formal proofs versus knowledge. It is an impressive feat to solve such a problem. However, because it is a Lean proof over millions of lines, it is going to take a while before the community gets real understanding, and validity of the proof. With an AI-independent approach available as well, it could present a great opportunity for discovery of new ideas and mathematics. We need to see how it all plays out.

There is another discussion to be had, which involves the role of frontier labs in research. Most of us see the potential benefits of this technology, but it is of utmost importance that we work towards a future where the agency is with the scientific community and not a couple of companies.

Mathematician Marcus Du Sautoy is anxious about what’s next for his field.Credit: David Levenson/Getty

Marcus Du Sautoy, mathematician and professor for the public understanding of science at the University of Oxford, UK.

It was real mix of emotions. A part of me says, how exciting to be alive when this great problem was solved! I think even when Fermat’s last theorem was solved, we had the same excitement and the same melancholy: that great motivator is gone.

Mixed in with that, is the complete surprise that it ended up being proved this way. If you’d asked me three months ago, I would never have predicted it.

There’s quite a lot of anxiety about what ‘math 2.0’ is going to look like.

Xin Zhang, assistant professor in mathematics at the University of Hong Kong.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03835-0

These interviews have been edited for length and clarity.

Correction 26 November 2026: This article originally described Harini Desiraju as a postdoctoral researcher; she is a lecturer in mathematics at the University of Warwick, UK.

#1141. Gordon double leads rotated Barcelona to 4-1 win in Baku without Lamine Yamal

Anthony Gordon scored twice as Hansi Flick's rotated Barcelona beat Sabah FK 4-1 in Baku without Lamine Yamal. The win lifts them to fourth in the Champions League league phase before Atlético Madrid and Manchester City visit.

In Baku, Barcelona completed the longest European away trip in their history and returned with a comfortable victory over Sabah FK. Hansi Flick rotated his side, and Lamine Yamal did not make the journey.

Joy-Lance Mickels scored a consolation goal for the Azerbaijani champions. Sabah had won only one of their first four league-phase matches. One of their defeats was a heavy loss to Manchester United.

Goalkeeper Stas Pokatilov failed to deal with an Adeyemi cross in the first half. Gordon was on hand to turn the ball in and put Barcelona ahead.

Flick said his side had more than 70% of possession in the first half. He was unhappy, though, with the easy mistakes his team made. He also noted that Sabah had nothing to lose.

The game was decided soon after the restart. Barcelona scored three times in the space of nine minutes. Gordon struck first, converting a rebound after Pokatilov saved from Jesus.

Four minutes later, Adeyemi finished Alejandro Balde’s cross. Jesus then made it four on the hour. He followed up after Jules Koundé’s header was saved.

The scoreline fits a side that controlled the ball for long spells.

The win also gave Flick room to manage his squad. Across 18 matches this season, Pedri had appeared every time, something no team-mate could match. He was taken off at half-time.

That decision had been agreed beforehand. Pedri was to play only the first 45 minutes whatever happened. Dani Olmo’s minutes were also limited to one half.

Resting key players in Baku could pay off over the coming fortnight. Barcelona are top of LaLiga and face two demanding fixtures at home.

The result keeps Barcelona on course for an automatic top-eight finish in the league phase. Manchester City sit eighth on 10 points. That makes the matchday 6 meeting a direct contest between two sides in the top eight.

Fantastic four. pic.twitter.com/Rbu25knoN4

— FC Barcelona (@FCBarcelona) November 26, 2026

City have not faced Barcelona at the Camp Nou since October 2016, the club said.

Before that, Barcelona turn to domestic business. They visit Deportivo de La Coruña on Sunday 29 November, then host Atlético Madrid in LaLiga at Spotify Camp Nou on Wednesday 2 December at 9.30pm CET.

#1140. Ten-man Bournemouth come from behind to beat Celta at Balaídos and top Europa League

Celta Vigo lost at home to Bournemouth even though the visitors played most of the game a man down. The defeat extends a difficult run for Claudio Giráldez's side, while the visitors moved to the top of the Europa League table.

Bournemouth came from behind to beat Celta Vigo 1-2 at the Municipal de Balaídos on Thursday 26 November 2026. With Javier Rueda García providing the assist for Aspas, Celta went into the break 1-0 up.

The game turned soon after the restart. Álvaro Rodríguez, the Uruguay international, headed Bournemouth level in the 47th minute from an Amine Adli assist. Rayan then scored the winner on a counter-attack in the 78th minute, set up by Marcus Tavernier. Aspas was booked for dissent in the same minute.

The match statistics show how much of the play Celta had. The hosts completed 527 passes from 607. Bournemouth completed 264 from 333. Fourteen of Celta’s attempts came from inside the box, against four for the visitors.

Celta’s finishing did not match that volume. They put five shots on target, while Bournemouth managed six. Seven Celta efforts were blocked and eight went wide. Celta goalkeeper Ionuț Radu made four saves.

Giráldez told EFE that his team did not show enough composure or intelligence to make use of the extra man after Diakité’s dismissal. In his view, Rodríguez’s equaliser brought back the anxiety of Celta’s poor run.

That run is visible in the results. Celta have won one of their last six games in all competitions, a 5-0 victory over Salamanca UDS. Before Bournemouth, they lost 1-2 to Real Madrid. They also drew 0-0 with Levante and lost to Union St. Gilloise and Rayo Vallecano.

Bournemouth’s recent run includes victories over Nottingham Forest, Ipswich, Leeds and Aston Villa.

The 2026/27 Europa League is the club’s debut in European competition. Before Vigo, they had beaten Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, AC Milan and Sparta Praha in the competition. Rodríguez was the top-rated player in the match, with a rating of 7.9.

Both sides return to league action on Sunday 29 November. Celta host Villarreal in LaLiga, while Bournemouth travel to Fulham in the Premier League.

Giráldez still believes Celta can win all three of their remaining league-phase games. The last two league-phase matchdays are on 21 and 28 January 2027. Before then, Celta travel to Olympique de Marseille on Thursday 10 December 2026, with kick-off at 18:45 Spanish time.

#1139. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

"Absolutely brilliant from Arsenal." Kai Havertz gives Arsenal an early lead at Anfield! ⚡️ https://t.co/eeyhRcLlel

After that? Liverpool swarmed over Arsenal, particularly in the first-half with Florian Wirtz’s free-kick cannoning back off the crossbar and Mac Allister somehow heading over. He was six yards out and unmarked, it was a glorious chance.

That was the hosts’ last tangible opportunity to score. As well as Arsenal defended, it was not a good afternoon for Liverpool’s forwards, Bradley Barcola in particular, although it was interesting to see Arsenal double-up on Rio Ngumoha when he came on. Arteta reacted by bringing on a second left-back, in Piero Hincapié.

Arsenal had the best chance with Alisson denying Christos Tzolis as the Greek winger’s low volley threatened to arc around him.

A brilliant save from Alisson to deny Tzolis! 🧤 https://t.co/0K2DPuUMEu

For Liverpool it became frantic. They could not surf the emotion, not against this battle-hardened Arsenal.

Boos rang out at the end – signs of how Arsenal had frustrated Liverpool – as Arteta gained his first win at Anfield as a manager. He was in the last Arsenal team to win here as a player 14 years ago. But this one meant more – that was also clear and obvious as he joyfully jumped into the arms of his assistant, Gabriel Heinze.

"You're supposed to make something of it!" "That's obvious that he's pulled his shirt, why does he need to dive?" Ian Wright and Daniel Sturridge discuss Alexander Isak's penalty appeal 💬 https://t.co/G0aa7tP92t

"It's a clear penalty" Andoni Iraola is adamant Liverpool should have been awarded a penalty for a foul on Alexander Isak ⤵️ https://t.co/hpaCeVVsbp

Pride? No disappointment. Disappointment. We played at home. We had some opportunities. Obviously we tried everything. We could have done better in the last 15 minutes to get balls in the box but it wasn’t enough. That’s why it’s a disappointment.

After we conceded we started to play much better. We created the big chance for Alexis which could have changed the game. It didn’t happen. We kept pushing and pushing.

I think there was also a clear penalty. I have seen it back. I’ve seen it being given on other occasions. [Should Alex have made more of it. Maybe the VAR doesn’t notice it…] The VAR doesn’t notice it? We have 50 cameras, even more. Why do you have to complain more if they have 50 cameras. They spotted it because everyone’s seen it. It wasn’t given, we lose the game. Congratulations to Arsenal.

When someone new comes in the building it just takes a bit if time. Our fans can see there is so much improvement and we work out socks off. What we do need as well is results.

Havertz: “It means a lot to the whole football club. It is important. It’s what they deserve [the fans]. We all know what this stadium is about. We knew it was coming but we all stuck together, defended together. Ninety per cent of the goal belongs to that man [Rice].”

Rice: “That’s the Anfield way. That is what Liverpool do. This stadium creates waves and waves of attacks. Relentless. That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I’ve never seen before. The manager had an honest conversation with me and said I could do even more for this club [in terms of assists and goals]. It’s always tiring coming here. First win in 14 years and my first win here too. It’s demanding. An amazing result. I have learnt that you can only take the table seriously in February and March and all you can do until then is win as many as you can.”

Barcola’s last-gasp cross is blocked and that is that.

Arsenal have won at Anfield for the first time since 2012.

Hincapié fouls Ngumoha in the Liverpool box. Alisson launches it and Gabriel throws himself on to the floor after a touch from Isak and Arsenal have a free-kick.

Isak is caught in the offside trap when chasing Barcola’s hook over the top that could have put him through one-on-one.

Barcola cannot impart any power on a shot from eight yards after he pounced following some pinball passes and ricochets. Raya easily stops it. A shot on target.

Munoz, sandwiched between Hincapie and Calafiori, manages to get his head on Koumas’s flick on at the back post bit cannot get any power on it.

Ngumoha’s shot is deflected behind for a corner.

Van Dijk is playing as a centre-forward now but Gyojkeres’ lack of pace ruins Arsenal’s chances of exploiting his absence at the back from a counter-attack when he can’t get to Lewis-Skelly’s upfield pass.

Calafiori blocks Ngumoha’s left-foot shot out for a throw-in.

Calafiori shins a pass into touch when under pressure from Ngumoha. Still no Liverpool shot on target.

Hincapié goes to left-back with Calafiori in front of him.

Koumas → AraujoMuñoz  → WirtzTsimikas → Kerkez

Mac Allister goes down clutching his head after winding up Arsenal with a slap on Odegaard. Madueke had narrowed the gap and touched Mac Allister’s forehead with his own but sanity prevails and Madueke is not sanctioned. Mac Allister and Timber are booked.

Liverpool keep huffing and puffing around the Arsenal box but the champions seem more and more convinced that their house is made of bricks.

You will go a long way this season before you see a better save than the one Alisson Becker has just produced to keep Liverpool in the contest. The speed and the reflexes to get down and turn Tzolis’s shot around the corner was breathtaking. A reminder, if it were needed, of what an impossible job Liverpool will have to replace him one day.

Van Dijk leathers a shot from 25 yards that loops up over to the right. Ngumoha chases it and keeps it in, working it back to MacAllister whose cross is plucked out of the air by Raya.

Superb save from Alisson low to his left to turn Tzolis’s blistering daisy-cutter round the post.

A brilliant save from Alisson to deny Tzolis! 🧤 https://t.co/0K2DPuUMEu

“It’s a joke, an absolute joke,” says Gary Neville about the protocol that kept Kerkez out of the game for a minute when hurt accidentally.

Van Dijk cuts out Tzolis’s pass from the left intended for Calafiori on an underlapping run into the box.

Liverpool defend the corner though at the price of going down to 10 because Kerkez went down after a collision of heads.

Tzolis wastes a golden opportunity on the break by opting not to shoot as Alisson came out to meet him but centre it for Odegaard instead. Jacquet put his foot in to divert it over the bar.

Barcola goes skipping down the left and manages to slide a pass through Timber’s legs for Wirtz, who has to stretch to control it, pirouettes and then wastes it 16 yards out, dead centre, by striking it into a defender. Kerkez stops a possible counter-attack with a foul on Madueke that puts him in the book.

Raya gives the ball away cheaply but the bounce is awkward for Barcola whose attempt to head it on for Isak is too loopy and gives the keeper the time to rush out and regather.

Arsenal waste a few seconds after Van Dijk was penalised for a foul on Bruno. They decide to take him off but even when the substitution is completed, they still dawdle over the restart.

Mac Allister, in shooting territory 25 yards out, tries to fizz a pass to Wirtz in the box instead and Arsenal scramble it away.

Both players receive rousing receptions on departure and entry.

The more you watch Jéremy Jacquet, the easier it is to understand why Liverpool made the decision to not follow up interest in Marc Guehi back in January. The young Frenchman has been – to borrow a phrase from his national team manager Zinedine Zidane – “very good; very, very good” since he was thrust into the team and he’s shown it again in this match.

Liverpool take the free-kick quickly and Kerkez releases Isak down the left to lash a left-foot shot over the angle of left post and crossbar.

Madueke is booked for legging up Barcola who threatened to race away on a counter after Van Dijk had blocked Bruno’s shot.

Arsenal hold their nerve and their lines when Wirtz, Nyoni and Gakpo try to thread passes in to feet in the penalty area, managing to make the blocks as Liverpool keep probing.

There’s a groan when Gakpo’s cross from the right hits Bruno. Then Isak was caught offside when turning the ball around the corner for Wirtz to have a shot.

Arsenal set up solidly in defensive lines to stop Liverpool raising the tempo on which they thrived in the first half.

Araujo wends his way around Calafiori after good work from Isak and crosses towards the penalty spot. Gabriel hooks the ball away with Wirtz and Isak on their heels around the 18-yard line.

Victor Muñoz has gone through a rigorous half-time warm up, which indicates he won’t be far away from getting minutes. The Spaniard’s pace and directness on the flank is exactly what Liverpool need in the second period. You would anticipate, too, there will come a point when Dominik Szoboszlai is introduced. Liverpool aren’t out of this, by any means, but they need a step up again.

Liverpool re-start “kicking into the Kop” in the words of Ian Wright. A ling chip down the right gives Gakpo something to chase but he can’t get round Calafiori who shepherds it out for a goal-kick.

Liverpool will be pleased with their response to going behind but very frustrated also at not, at least, being level. Arsenal started superbly and got their goal but Liverpool have swarmed all over them since. It has been a bit too frantic at times. There have been a series of penalty appeals, most of which were rightly ignored. But Arsenal got away with one when Jurrien Timber clearly pulled at Alexander Isak’s shirt, preventing him from heading a cross. It is the kind of incident that really makes you wonder what the VAR is doing.

Arsenal have been on the ropes since opening the scoring as wave after wave of Liverpool attacks swarm towards their box. But so far they retain their lead but will have to adjust their midfield and forward lines soon as it’s been boy stood on the burning deck stuff from Rice at times. Mac Allister, who has become a beast in the air recently, should have equalised but seemed to stoop into it and get under it rather than heading it down.

Barcola is booked for catching Timber in a sliding tackle and his visible contempt for the decision means there will be no reprieve.

With two minutes of stoppage time signalled Arsenal are on a rare attack but Tozolis again doesn’t release the ball when he should and slows it down.

Liverpool seem intent on trying to score a perfect goal. The irony is that it’s old fashioned pace and being direct that is starting to unsettle Arsenal. Bradley Barcola, therefore, needs to step up. He’s been on the edges so far and it’s crying out for him to have a persistent run at Jurrien Timber and ask him some big questions.

Mac Allister misses a sitter. He eluded his midfield marker and met Kerkez’s perfect cross between the penalty spot and six-yard line but steered it over. Now it’s Calafiori’s turn to upbraid the players ahead of him.

Rice is becoming very annoyed about a lack of support from his front players in providing a viable outlet when he wins the ball. He is waving his arms and chuntering away.

Wirtz takes the free-kick bending it with dip and whip over Raya but into the heart of the crossbar. Arsenal butcher their counter-attacking opportunity.

Timber is penalised for a decent-looking tackle on Isak just outside the box on the Liverpool left. That comes a moment after the referee gave Liverpool a corner despite Mac Allister’s cross not touching an Arsenal player. They are going spare and one can sympathise with them.

There’s no room at all in the Arsenal penalty area as first Mac Allister tries to fizz a pass through the massed ranks then Isak weaves an opening for a left-foot shot that he smacks into the hoardings, 3ft wide and rising.

Arsenal enjoy a moment of respite on a rapid counter down the right but Bruno takes too many touches when found by Odegaard in the middle, 18 yards out, allowing Mac Allister to tie him up.

Sky digs out a replay from the 21st minute which clearly shows Timber with a fistful of Isak’s shirt that stopped him reaching a cross. But he, unlike the bench, did not appeal for a penalty. “He is nice,” says Gary Neville disdainfully.

Kerkez cushions a pass on his thigh when he ghosts into the centre-forward position and then tamely lobs a volley wide from 18 yards. Liverpool are swarming the Arsenal penalty area.

Liverpool are laying siege at the moment, snapping into tackles, putting in crosses, taking one too many touches to surprise Arsenal. Now Gakpo goes down in the box when confronted by Tzolis who does make contact but not enough for Madley or the VAR after a look.

Liverpool corner from the right. Van Dijk wins the header and Isak, creeping round Konsa, is there to tap it in, but Raya is alert and pushes it behind before Isak can pounce.

Tzoli’s cross from the left is met at the back post by Timber who tries to knock it back across the six-yard box to Havertz but Timber gets in the way.

Mac Allister’s crossfield pearler picks out Kerkez but he hits the first defender with his cross and Arsenal counter at pace and Madueke faces Kerkez up but dawdles instead of trying to dribble past him. He waits for reinforcements and then cuts it back to Bruno who bends a pass through the six-yard box from the right of the D that Tzolis slides in but just cannot reach

The Arsenal goal has been a real tonic for Liverpool who are now hounding Arsenal’s players when in possession and gorging on mistakes, roared on by a raucous crowd. The volume is as high as I’ve heard for ages.

Two close shaves for Arsenal immediately after the goal, Rice needing to get back to stop Konsa’s mistake giving Wirtz a path to goal and then Barcola fades a cross/shot from the left of the D just beyond the right post.

Liverpool 0 Arsenal 1 (Havertz) Odegaard who, with Rice and Bruno, have dominated midfield, triggers the press when Liverpool play out from the back, disrupting a pass then running back to collect his interception. He strolls forward and plays it to Madueke who waits for Rice’s run on the overlap. The England midfielder delivers perfectly from the right and Havertz is Johnny on the spot at the back post to crash a shot past the scrambling Alisson.

"Absolutely brilliant from Arsenal." Kai Havertz gives Arsenal an early lead at Anfield! ⚡️ https://t.co/eeyhRcLlel

Van Dijk semi-deliberately collides with Havertz after clearing the ball very forcefully.

#1138. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

#1137. Atlético beat Viking 2-0 as both strikers score, but Sørloth injury hits Barcelona trip

Alexander Sørloth and Julián Álvarez both ended goal droughts as Atlético Madrid beat Viking FK 2-0 to reach seven points in the Champions League. Sørloth's muscle injury now adds to an injury list that already includes Lookman, just as Atlético face Barcelona and PSV.

Atlético Madrid’s win over Viking FK revived their hopes of a direct top-eight finish. Three league-phase games remain, and one of them is away to PSV. Both of Simeone’s leading strikers found the net. Yet the night also added a new name to the injury list.

Sørloth broke the deadlock by firing in a pass from Alejandro Grimaldo. Five minutes later, Álvarez’s free-kick crept in at the near post. It was his 27th goal in the Champions League. It was also his first Champions League goal at the Metropolitano in 210 days. The strike was his third of the 2026-27 season: one in LaLiga and two in Europe.

Grimaldo was named Player of the Match. Viking defender Henrik Falchener was sent off late in the game.

The result follows an uneven league phase. Atlético opened with a 2-1 defeat at Liverpool. They then beat Manchester United 2-0 at home. A 1-1 draw at Stuttgart followed. Bayern München then won 0-2 at the Metropolitano on 3 November.

That home defeat was unusual. Before kick-off against Viking, Atlético had won 11 of their previous 14 home matches in the group stage or league phase. They lost the other three. The victory over the Norwegian side returned them to winning ways in front of their own supporters.

The mood inside the stadium was not entirely positive, however. Some home fans whistled Álvarez when he was substituted, even though he had scored.

Sørloth went off limping after 71 minutes. He had taken a heavy knock against the post and left the field with an overload, the club said on 26 November. No date has been set for his return. He will do physiotherapy and gym rehabilitation.

The expected absence is significant. ESPN Deportes expects him to miss at least the games against Elche, Barcelona, Real Betis, Valencia and PSV. That would rule him out of the visit to Eindhoven.

#1136. Hoops hero Duran keen to repay 'incredible' Celtic supporters

Published: 08:23 EST, 28 November 2026 | Updated: 08:30 EST, 28 November 2026

Celtic striker Camilo Duran is determined to keep repaying supporters after achieving hero status already.

The Colombia international scored his 15th goal since his summer move from Qarabag when he headed a late Europa League winner against Torreense on Thursday.

About 4,000 travelling fans hailed the 24-year-old in Portugal and he told Celtic Player: 'They’ve been incredible. Since I came here, they have been giving me confidence and support. So I always try to do better for them and getting the win for them is the biggest way to give back.'

Duran hit five Champions League goals last season for Qarabag as a centre-forward but was initially played on the wing at Celtic to accommodate the arrival of club record signing Kasper Hogh.

But with Hogh now without a goal in 17 club games, Duran has firmly established himself as Celtic’s main striker following his prolific form, whether through the middle or out wide.

And the South American has felt the faith of manager Martin O’Neill.

'He has been really, really calm about it and he has been giving me confidence,' Duran said. 'I will just try to bring it on the pitch and to perform very well.'

Celtic have fresh fitness doubts over Dane Murray and Hogh ahead of Sunday’s trip to Hearts, while Benjamin Nygren is nursing a heel problem.

Camilo Duran has scored 15 goals already since signing for Celtic from Qarabag

The Hoops hammered Hearts 7-1 last month but Jambos boss Wouter Vrancken feels his team are ready to deliver a much-improved display this time around after an encouraging first week back since the latest international break.

The Tynecastle side’s injury crisis has started to ease, with Blair Spittal, Ageu, Rogers Mato and Christian Borchgrevink all back, and they are buoyed by an 8-0 win at Dundee last weekend and an impressive performance in Thursday’s agonising 3-2 defeat at home to Monaco in the Conference League.

'We played two good games and two good performances against good sides, especially Thursday, and that gives you the confidence,' said Vrancken.

'But still we are playing against a good side with only two days’ rest, so we have to manage fatigue and make sure that we are as fresh as possible again to make up for what happened a few weeks ago, and especially because it’s a home game.'

Vrancken is not anticipating any of his other injured players to be ready to return on Sunday.

Yang Ji is in the Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China, and at the Key University Laboratory of Metabolism and Health of Guangdong, Southern University of Science and Technology.

Peng George Wang is in the Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China, and at the Key University Laboratory of Metabolism and Health of Guangdong, Southern University of Science and Technology.

Long chains of sugars known as polysaccharides support many biological functions, from strengthening tissues to modulating cell signalling. Synthesizing these compounds in the laboratory with precise lengths and architectures, which are needed to establish how the structures of polysaccharides affect biological behaviour, has been difficult. Writing in Nature, Yin et al.1 now report an enzyme-based strategy that produces highly uniform polysaccharides and enables chains to restart growth after consuming all of the sugar building blocks in the reaction, once more sugars are added. The authors achieved this control by adjusting how readily an enzyme binds the small sugar molecules that are used to initiate the growth of each chain.

#1134. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

#1133. Will the real Hearts please stand up? Cut to pieces by Celtic, then destroyers of Dundee... you never know what you are going to get with Vrancken's side

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 09:21 EST, 28 November 2026 | Updated: 09:23 EST, 28 November 2026

In what is proving to be a rollercoaster of a season for Hearts, it is still too early to pass any definitive judgment on whether Wouter Vrancken will be a success as head coach.

Hamstrung by such an extensive injury list and missing so many key players, the Belgian would be entitled to feel like he has been operating with one hand tied behind his back for much of the campaign.

It has largely been a case of make do and mend over these past couple of months, an effort to try and scrape by and eke out results by whatever means possible until such times they can return to a clean bill of health.

Yet, although the long-term picture under Vrancken remains unclear, one thing is for sure. It certainly won’t be dull. Hearts will be nothing if not entertaining.

Sabri Guendouz celebrates his goal in Hearts' 8-0 win at Dundee

In the space of just over a month, they have recorded a 7-1 defeat and an 8-0 victory domestically in the Scottish Premiership; humiliation at Celtic Park and an annihilation of Dundee at Dens Park.

That in itself is quite remarkable. When would you ever see a team losing 7-1 and winning 8-0 not only in the same season, but only a few weeks apart?

The 3-2 defeat to Monaco at Tynecastle in the UEFA Conference League on Thursday night was another case in point of just how thrillingly unpredictable Vrancken’s team can be.

Hearts went 1-0 up early in the game, then fell 2-1 behind, equalised on the cusp of half-time, thought they had won a penalty in the second half, then lost a late goal in stoppage-time.

That was the game in a nutshell on a night when Vrancken’s patched-up side almost claimed what would have been an excellent point against the French giants.

But it has been the performances of Jordi Altena which have really caught the eye of late. He has been excellent in a period when Hearts have really needed players to step up.

Altena scored the opening goal against Monaco — and an absolute screamer it was, too. Finally, Hearts fans are starting to see the player they thought they had signed back in January.

When Altena arrived at Tynecastle back at the turn of the year, he was pitched in for an immediate debut against Livingston and had an excellent game as Hearts won 1-0.

Jamie McCart scores an own goal in Hearts' humiliating 7-1 loss at Celtic Park

Toiling-up for a crack at winning the title in the second half of the season, the belief was that he would add real class and attacking intent from right-back.

Yet, bizarrely, Derek McInnes seemed unsure. Altena would only start three more league matches across the second half of last season.

Sabah Kerjota was another example of a player strangely under-utilised by McInnes. He did not start a single match last season, with every one of his 19 appearances coming off the bench as a substitute.

Now, like Altena, Kerjota is also lighting it up. Kerjota’s goal against Monaco was equally fabulous and the reluctance from McInnes to use him last season just looks increasingly odd.

Having spent last season largely on the fringes, these two players have now stepped out of the shadows and are emerging as key men for Vrancken.

Their stories are particularly compelling. Only two years ago, Altena was playing in the third-tier in Holland with De Treffers.

One season followed with RKC Waalwijk in the second tier before the Jamestown Analytics system flagged him up as a transfer target for Hearts.

Dutch utility player Jordi Altena has been in fine form for Hearts this season

Kerjota, meanwhile, was playing in the lower leagues in Italy before making the move to Gorgie. He, too, looks to be a player of good ability.

There is a separate argument to be had about Jamestown and about just how many of their signings so far at Hearts have been a resounding success.

Yet, particularly in the case of Altena, it looks increasingly likely that Hearts have unearthed a terrific talent, one who is comfortable playing across a number of positions.

Altena is a right-back by trade, but he has already shown that he is more than capable of playing more centrally and also in midfield.

‘I’m playing quite a lot now if I compare to last season, I feel like I’m improving every week,' said the Dutchman recently.

‘I’m young, so I think that’s personally the most important thing, and I’m happy that I keep getting better and better. I feel like my ceiling is quite high.’

Altena will turn 23 next week. His best years are still very much to come. If Vrancken can implement his high-octane style and find a greater level of consistency, Altena could shine.

This afternoon’s clash with Celtic at Tynecastle will not only be a good gauge of his progress, but also how Hearts have developed overall under Vrancken.

When they were hammered 7-1 at Parkhead earlier in the season, they were wide-open at the back and exposed all too easily.

They went man-for-man with how they tried to press Celtic and it backfired spectacularly. Not only that, Vrancken’s refusal to change anything during the match was most alarming.

Nobody doubts this Celtic team are hugely vulnerable. They are a mess. The performance in Portugal on Thursday night as they laboured to a 2-1 win over second-tier Torreense was dreadful.

Hearts should look to be aggressive and get after them again. But they need to pick and choose their moments more intelligently than they did when the teams met in Glasgow.

Wouter Vrancken has had to deal with an injury crisis in his first season at Hearts

If Hearts are to have any hope of clawing their way back into the title race this season, it is surely a match they must win.

They currently sit 11 points behind Celtic with a game in hand. It still feels like a long shot, but victory this afternoon might just start to fuel some belief again.

The confidence they would have taken from last week’s demolition of Dundee is bound to do them a power of good, given that Celtic are there for the taking.

In Altena and Kerjota, Hearts have two players who have gone from bit-part roles last season to now very much being the main men.

Given the humiliation Hearts suffered last time out against Celtic, they wouldn’t be human if they didn’t feel a burning sense of revenge.

And that’s not even to mention what happened on the final day of last season...

Games between these two rarely disappoint. This promises to be another thriller. Hearts and Vrancken are racking up a few of those.

#1132. How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community

As the co-founder of the ADIRA Drag Festival, Lebanese performance artist, drag performer, DJ and cultural organizer Hassandra has become an essential part of Berlin's queer artistic landscape.

"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.

Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.

Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.

"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person."

The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.

Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.

"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."

Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.

In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.

Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.

Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.

As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.

That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.

"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."

Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."  "There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.

The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

#1131. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.
