#1059. Mikel Arteta defends Arsenal's attack, but league numbers reveal a real Premier League slump

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Mikel Arteta wants it. His supporters certainly do. His players look like they might one of these days. So why aren't Arsenal cutting loose and running up the goals? Why, in fact, aren't they even scoring at the rate of last season, when every goal had to be dragged kicking and screaming into the opposition net?

Through 18 games this season across all competitions, the English champions have 30 goals to their name, a scoring rate that is a fair way below the 2025-26 campaign, when their 114 goals in all competitions came at a rate of 1.81 per game. This early in 2026-27, there could be a very quick and easy answer to any questions about Arsenal's attack. It might just be variance. That's what Arteta would argue.

"I think we have improved in every stat," he said, "apart from probably the amount of goals that we have scored. It's been quite similar, we had a period that it was much higher [in 2023-24]. Premier League, Champions League, we can debate that as well.

"There is an element as well of luck, how the hell the ball bounces on the post two times when the ball is there and it doesn't go in [as it did for Borussia Dortmund's Serhou Guirassy in Tuesday's 1-1 draw in the Champions League], nobody can explain that. We will do what is in our hand to do, fully trust the players and the quality that we have to go and deliver every three days."

Is Arteta right? Have Arsenal improved in every stat except the one that decides the final score? Well, it rather depends on how you slice the data. Throw everything from 2025-26, 2026-27 and even a few of the preceding years into a big old analytics stew, and you'd have to say there are signs of improvement across all competitions. Shots per game are up from 14.6 to 15.9, touches in the box going up over 10% to 36.8 per game. Expected goals are on the up at 1.8 per game too. If all those numbers are on the up, then it's fair to assume goals will follow.

There might be an issue to consider, though, when we compare an all-competitions 2026-27 data set with all competitions from completed seasons. Right now, Arsenal's extra non-Premier League games are relatively low-stakes games, often (though not exclusively) against relatively low-standard opposition. If we want to be as close as we can be to comparing apples with apples, we might be best off looking solely at events in the Premier League.

In those games, the picture looks different. As the graphic above illustrates, there were periods in the title-winning season where Arsenal lacked the threat they pose even in a down moment now. In the aggregate, however, it is clear in which season they looked to be the more dangerous team. Their 13.7 shots per game is one fewer than last season, their xG down from 1.71 to 1.6. Both are their lowest in any league season under Arteta since his first full one in 2020-21. So too the goal tally, as they trend toward a 59-goal season.

It is hard to believe you can win a title scoring so few, even if your defense is as otherworldly as the Gunners'. There are all sorts of off-field questions about Manchester City coloring this title race -- and they may be bleeding onto the field -- but if a team is trending toward nearly 20 more goals and has a non-penalty xG difference that is 10% better, it would be unwise to count it out.

Statistically, then, Arsenal's attack looks like being an inhibiting factor for their prospects this season. What is curious about that is, at least compared to what was served up last season, this feels like a better team to watch. Of course, there are the Nottingham Forest away sort of matches where you've seen young men have more sustained success building flat-pack furniture without the instruction manual and what's that, the Allen key wasn't in the box. Those matches probably tell you as much about the Premier League as Arsenal. Such is the depth of athletic talent in the English top flight; it really is quite hard to find gaps in well-drilled low blocks before your opponent plugs them.

What is curious, though, about Arsenal's struggles is that so many of the factors that seemed to be inhibiting them last season have eased this season. The unbearable weight of not being champions has been lifted off their shoulders. Player availability is better than it was. The football looks good. Martin Odegaard is the creative force he was before injuries hobbled him last season. As in 2025-26, Bukayo Saka is missing, but this time Noni Madueke has stepped up, leading the Premier League in combined shots and chances created per 90 minutes. Kai Havertz is fit, Viktor Gyokeres has improved, and Bruno Guimaraes' defensive flaws are partially offset by his fizzing passes through the line. It's only really in the last few weeks that it has felt like a downgrade on the left to have swapped out Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli for Christos Tzolis plus more minutes from Eberechi Eze.

At their best, Arsenal are fun in a way they could never have been amid the neuroses that were the price of a first title in 22 years. That much was apparent on Tuesday as they laid down 30 shots on Bundesliga leaders Dortmund. Only the best attacks can run up those sorts of numbers; you would suppose that quality would bleed into Premier League games, especially when it followed on from an outstanding first half at Newcastle.

It even seems that Arsenal have begun to address what Arteta saw as the issue bedeviling not only his team in 2025-26 but the sport as a whole: man-to-man marking. Asked in March if he feared that a swing toward set pieces was breaking the sport, he insisted that players following their opponent up and down the pitch was "the biggest issue" in the Premier League. Unlike the meat-wall era (RIP), teams are still embracing man-to-man defenses. This season, however, it seems Arsenal have found another way of manipulating that.

Arteta had always rolled out lineups with plenty of positional versatility. That has been supercharged lately, particularly with his fullbacks, as Jurrien Timber pops up on the left wing and Piero Hincapie takes the Riccardo Calafiori roles to extremes, stretching the Dortmund defensive line while Gyokeres dropped deep in midweek. Add to that the freedom for Tzolis to roam from one flank to the other, and you have a team that, at least out wide, is more prepared than ever to test the limits of the opposition's man-to-man system. If Harvey Barnes is going to stick with Timber, he's going to have to do it to the ends of the earth, or at least St. James' Park.

"We're trying to find the right solutions and adjusting to the profile of players we have and the types of challenges and jobs that the opponent will offer on the day," Arteta said. "I think the understanding of what we have to do and the timings are much better. We have been much more efficient up to the point of actually scoring the goal, and making the most of the action."

That fluidity is probably why it feels like Arsenal are more threatening as an attacking force, vibes being fundamentally an open-play concept. And when the ball is live, this team is as good as it has been in years. In all competitions, Arsenal have more xG from open play than in any season since 2023-24, the year they blitzed their way to 91 Premier League goals. They are in double figures for open-play shots too, again something they only achieved in their early years of title contention.

The same question again, then. If it looks so right on the pitch, why isn't it translating into goals? It's tempting to conclude that this is a team that is a little too happy to settle for a one-goal winning margin, even if its manager insists that is not the case.

"I prefer to win by five, or six, or seven, for sure," Arteta said. "I'm going to enjoy the game much more, especially the last few minutes. The boys are going to have more fun. I think scoring goals is ultimately what creates a good feeling, joy, happiness, celebration around the stands. It's the most important thing in football, apart from winning.

"When the margin is by one goal, especially with the level of the opponent that we play every three days, how difficult it is; they just need a moment, and it happened with Dortmund. They broke the press after eliminating one of our front players, and they have the capacity to pick out that player, that player has an individual action, and then it's a goal. They didn't do much more than that, but that was enough to get a point and you have to assume that [they might do that]."

Do Arteta's players assume that? He will tell you that his players don't ever take a "what we have, we hold" approach on purpose. Even he seemed to acknowledge, though, that Arsenal's past success at grinding out tight wins might be playing on their minds. It's reflected in the data. Part of the reason why the xG totals might be so low at the Emirates is that this team spends so much time leading. And when they're leading, they are a below-average attack that averages just 1.22 xG per 90.

If you've watched Arsenal in the last few years, that data point will ring true. Arsenal back themselves to hold out against any attack. For most teams, holding on to a one-goal margin is so risky as to be about as cavalier as chasing a second. Most teams aren't anchored by Gabriel, William Saliba and Ezri Konsa.

"I don't think that's something we do purposely," Arteta said when asked if Arsenal are too comfortable leading by a goal. "Sometimes you have to give credit to the opposition when they are able to do that. Especially in the last few minutes, they take so many chances so if we don't finish the game off, they still have the belief they can get something from the game.

"The reality is that we have managed those kind of games really well in the last three or four years."

As for the other reason why the data is not quite so enamored with Arsenal's attack, well, it's also in that graphic above. The set-piece offense that launched a thousand moral panics is, well, not even average anymore. Earlier in the season, the tale of Arsenal's dead-ball attack was one of a team still creating a lot of chances but not converting them. It's still the case that they could have done more with what they had, 3.73 xG resulting in one goal, but as this season rolls on, they are creating fewer and fewer.

More corners are going short, more from the right are being loosely tossed at the near post without the fizz and whip that Declan Rice and Saka put on them, and far fewer are finding Gabriel attacking the ball in the center of the penalty area. Opponents are also giving up fewer corners -- a league-wide trend for which Arsenal are doubtless one of the causes -- with the 5.4 Arsenal are getting per game their fewest in six years. That is not much lower than last season's figure, though, and in 2025-26 Arsenal turned their 5.7 corners per game into an average of two shots. Now it's down at 1.3.

What was once one of the best offensive weapons in the league has been neutered, either by Arsenal's own deliberate design or a belief that referees would call them for blocks and screens that were deemed legitimate last season.

Where the goals and chances come from, then, has changed quite significantly. Perhaps that is not a bad thing. Arsenal rode the set-piece train as far as it would take them and now they have adjusted. This is a team that controls possession better than it used to, that is tilting the field like it always did but increasing the time and touches it gets in the attacking third. The goals haven't come yet and perhaps they never will at the volume that Arteta and his supporters might like. Still, when there is so little being given up at the other end, that is hardly an intractable problem.

#1058. Inter Miami's surprise playoff exit exposes the challenges of building a cohesive team around Lionel Messi

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Inter Miami came into the campaign with ambitions of winning back-to-back MLS Cup titles, but it quickly became clear that they had taken a step back following the retirement of Jordi Alba and Sergio Busquets. Lionel Messi still did Messi things, but it wasn't enough to save a season where the Herons employed three different coaches while failing to christen the Nu Stadium with a trophy. Miami may be a victim of their own standards, but the season has to go down as a failure, even if the Columbus Crew were impressive in pulling off their first-round victory.

It can be hard to match the highs of a season that saw a team make the knockouts of the Club World Cup and then win MLS Cup, but this season didn't come close despite an eye-watering spend bringing in German Berterame and Casemiro while completing transfer obligations on Rodrigo De Paul, Tadeo Allende and others in the squad.

There's a strange balance because just when it seems as if Miami are building around young, dynamic players looking to play alongside Messi en route to eventual European dreams, they're then dragged back into signing aging players who can't keep up with the pace of MLS. That leads to fun games to watch, but it doesn't lead to sustainable soccer, as when Messi doesn't lead the charge, Miami can't win games.

The Argentine didn't have a goal contribution in eight MLS games that he appeared in this season, including the playoffs. Miami failed to win any of those, with four losses and four draws. That doesn't seem like a team that is anywhere near prepared for the eventual life after Messi that will come for us all. We've already seen him retire from international play, and at 39, the day could come sooner than we think for the end of his club career as well.

Miami's time with Messi has been successful, winning the Leagues Cup, Supporters' Shield and MLS Cup, but the absolute avalanche of trophies expected when you have Messi hasn't come yet. With it being a salary-cap league, there are limits to building a super team, but Miami have come as close as any squad to doing it on paper. Yet it was still the collective brilliance of Nashville SC that stood out this season, and not the Herons.

Sure, Nashville may not win MLS Cup either, but looking at Nashville, what they do is repeatable, while Miami aren't. This is because there's a clear plan for what type of players Nashville target, and their focus on defense will ensure that Nashville's floor is high. They still have stars, but those stars are involved in every aspect of play instead of just the attack. When you can get Messi, you get Messi, but Miami have failed at building a cohesive team around him. When Messi eventually departs, there will be plenty of money to sink into their next star, but that star won't transcend soccer in the way that Messi has.

Due to that, an actual plan is needed on what to do moving forward. Significant resources are tied up in De Paul and Casemiro, while Berterame may need to be moved on to get a secondary goal scorer. Left back is still an issue, and the list keeps growing during a critical offseason for Miami. With the MLS Sprint season coming before the change to a traditional fall-to-spring soccer calendar, it's the perfect time for a much-needed reset. Manager Kily Gonzalez admitted that reliance on Messi played a part in the loss to Columbus, and priority number one for whoever the coach is will be to fix that. Getting back to what they did well in recruiting in South America is possible, but to do that, Miami need to commit to an identity. As this season showed, just firing a coach when things get tough and hoping that Messi can pull a team through isn't enough to win MLS Cup. Even with 42 goal contributions and a likely league MVP coming his way, Messi can only go so far. Miami need to figure out how to win without him, or this team is going back to what it was before Messi, a side struggling to even make the playoffs in a more competitive MLS.

#1057. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

United were left to rue two abysmal refereeing calls that meant they had to settle for a draw

A night that started with an enormous penalty save ended in agony as he had a rush of blood to give a second penalty away and even worse in the second half, dropped what should have been a simple catch to gift Suarez his second. Booked.

Simply not good enough. Dreadful defending which left Lammens exposed to concede the second penalty. Did little to stake his claim for minutes at the weekend against Brentford.

A sign of how strong his mentality is in that he responded brilliantly after being sent off so early at Anfield. Comfortably looks to be the defender Mauricio Pochettino can rely on the most.

A steadying presence at a time when United are crying out for a sense of calm at the back. His insertion into the starting XI coincided with a much more organised and solid approach. No coincidence.

Harry Maguire's leadership is absolutely vital at a time when United are crying out for calm

Could count himself unlucky to give away a first half penalty for loosely dangling a leg but he redeemed himself by winning one at the other end for United’s first goal. Learning on the job at left back but looks much better than whoever lines up on the right.

Staggeringly he was booked for winning the ball at the end of the first half which saw a valid Amad goal chalked off. Then was deservedly booked in the second, as United had a player sent off AGAIN. Will miss the next game versus RB Leipzig.

Proves to be so neat and tidy on the ball without being flash that his contribution can sometimes go unnoticed. Kept it simple and boy do United need more players doing that.

Talk about rotten luck after putting the ball in the net, ending a goal drought for United stretching back to December 2025, it was erroneously chalked off by dreadful officiating. He’s the busy bee-type player that Pochettino is going to love.

Does what top players do and puts his team on his back at the most crucial of moments. Coolest head in the stadium to convert the penalty and then the help of a fortunate divot two minutes later allowed him to end a 12-game drought for an open play goal.

Bruno Fernandes put the team on his back with a two-minute brace in the second half

Started in a less familiar role off the left before shifting centrally when Zirkzee was withdrawn, Mbeumo didn’t have too many opportunities to shine. Made sure he helped Martinez out defensively.

Has a new lease of life since Pochettino’s arrival and looks like he will actually get a fair shot at minutes with a focal point key to what his new head coach wants to do. Needs to cut out the silly flicks on the edge of his own box, though.

Walks away relieved as much as delighted to have kickstarted his tenure – finally. That being said, Pochettino will be tearing his hair out at the egregious mistakes from match officials again threatening to derail his side.
